OV-1

High-level operational concept

What the platform does, for whom, and across which trust boundaries. The customer configures a target, Litmus generates adversarial traffic from AWS and fires it at that target, scores the responses, and returns findings, a report and notifications. The loop closes when the team re-scans.

OV-1 diagramoperational concept, seven steps across four zones
Viewthe same diagram, with or without the line under each name
Call flow, step by stepthe same seven steps, read top to bottom

OV-1 shows where things sit. This shows when they happen. Every component that takes part gets a lane, time runs downward, and each numbered row is one hop between two of them. The numbers are the same as on OV-1, so the two read together.

How separate the orchestrator and the scan tasks really arewhat the account enforces, and what it does not

The tags on the diagram say what is verifiable. The orchestrator can reach every tenant. A scan task exists for one scan and is then destroyed. That separation is real, but it is narrower than a control plane and data plane split, so the diagram does not claim one.

YES
Execution is separatedThe orchestrator runs as long-lived services: FastAPI behind the ALB, plus Celery workers and Beat. Each scan runs as its own Fargate task, created for that scan and destroyed when it finishes. A scan task holds no tenancy or entitlement logic. It receives one config file scoped to one scan and it serves no user request.
YES
Reach is separatedOnly a scan task sends adversarial traffic to a customer endpoint. The API never calls a customer AI. Only the deep task calls Bedrock. In the other direction, the orchestrator is the only component that can read across tenants, because it is the only one that touches the organizations, users and subscriptions tables.
NO
Network and storage are sharedBoth run in the same private app subnet in one VPC, and both leave through the same NAT gateway. There is no subnet or security group boundary between the API service and the scan tasks. They share one RDS instance, one Redis cluster and one S3 bucket, and the scan config holding the target credentials sits in that same bucket as the reports.
NO
Identity is sharedAU8 is a single IAM task role, shared by every tenant’s scan. It grants RunTask and SES send alongside S3 and Bedrock invoke, so a scan container carries permissions it has no reason to hold. Progress callbacks authenticate with one shared SSM token rather than a per-task identity, which is why mTLS on that hop is still listed as proposed.
SO
Why the diagram avoids the termControl plane and data plane implies a boundary the platform enforces. Here the API also stages target credentials, returns findings and mints report links, so it handles customer data as well as arranging work. The accurate claim is execution isolation for each scan, not plane separation. On the reference architecture, "control plane call" still marks an AWS API call such as ECS RunTask, which is the correct use of the term. If the task roles are split and the scan tasks move to their own subnet and security group, the stronger claim becomes true and the labels can change.
Reading the labels, and how the control plane worksper tenant, per scan, shared, and the six calls that launch a scan

The three labels answer two different questions at once, which is why they are easy to confuse. Who owns the thing, and how long it lives. Read them together and the diagram becomes unambiguous.

?
The difference in one lineOwnership: per tenant means one customer, per scan means one run belonging to one customer, shared means everyone. Lifetime: per tenant lasts as long as the account, shared lasts as long as the deployment, per scan lasts minutes. Ephemeral is a statement about lifetime only, and on this diagram the only ephemeral things are the two scan tasks. The rule that resolves most confusion: nothing that is per tenant is compute, and no compute is per tenant.
PER TENANT
Created once at signup, lasts as long as the accountRecords only. An Auth0 Organization, which becomes the tenant identity for the life of the account and never changes. Rows in organizations and users. A Stripe customer and subscription. A reserved key prefix in the shared S3 bucket. No container, queue, database, cache or KMS key is created for a new customer, so a customer who never scans consumes no compute.
PER SCAN
Created at launch, destroyed at exit, which is what ephemeral meansOne Fargate task for a basic scan, two for a deep scan. Drawn with a dashed outline. The task is created when the scan starts, runs 5 to 30 minutes, exits and is gone. It belongs to one run of one customer, so ten scans from the same customer means ten tasks created and destroyed. The task carries no tenancy logic and serves no user request.
SHARED
Created once at deploy, lasts as long as the deploymentThe Orchestrator, which is two long-lived ECS services rather than tasks. One RDS Postgres instance, one ElastiCache Redis cluster, one S3 bucket, one KMS key per store, one global platform_config row. These come up before any customer exists. Adding a customer adds rows, not capacity, and the platform scales on load rather than on customer count.
CP
Yes, the Orchestrator is the control plane. Here is howThe control plane is the FastAPI and Celery half of the box, not the stores beneath it, and the line across the bottom of the box is the sequence it runs on every scan: authenticate the caller against the Auth0 JWKS, check the tier and the scan:write permission, write the scans row at status pending and return a scan_id, stage the config YAML into the S3 configs prefix, call ECS RunTask to launch the task or tasks with no customer data in the call, then queue a Celery job that polls ECS every fifteen seconds until the scan finishes. Every one of those six arranges work. None of them sends a prompt to a customer endpoint. The caveat to state in a questionnaire: the same FastAPI also returns findings and mints report links, so it handles customer data too and is not a pure control plane.
S3
Yes, the S3 bucket is sharedOne bucket for all customers. Each has a {client_id}/ prefix inside it, with a folder for each scan beneath that holding the config, the report.json and the report.html. The prefix is the isolation boundary and it is enforced in application code rather than by a bucket policy. The scan task role can reach the whole bucket today, which is why the Model view recommends an IAM condition on the prefix.
API
What FastAPI and Celery actually areFastAPI is the Python web framework the API runs on, served by Uvicorn on port 8000 behind the load balancer. It handles anything that fits inside a single request. Celery is a Python job queue for work that outlives a request. A scan takes minutes, so the API does not wait: it puts a job in Redis, and a worker polls ECS, parses the report into findings, then sends the email and the webhook. Celery Beat is the scheduler beside it, dispatching due scan schedules once a minute. Both are long-lived services, which is exactly what separates them from the two scan tasks.

The Model view carries the full list: how a tenant is created in ten steps, twelve objects with where each one lives and how it is isolated, and six ways to harden the model. Open the Model view.

Reference architecture with analysis overlays

One diagram, seven readings. The base drawing shows subnet placement, the single ingress path and the single egress path. The numbered sequence is always on, so the base drawing already reads as a flow. Each overlay then fades that base, answers a different review question and prints its own key at the foot of the drawing: what moves, what is stored and how sensitive it is, what protocol carries it, what encrypts it, how it maps to the Well-Architected pillars, and which security controls sit where.

Sequence of events: what flows from where12 hops, each with the data it carries

The pastel numbers on the diagram mark where data changes hands. For a threat model what matters is not the call order but the payload on each hop and which side of the boundary it ends up on.

1
CloudFront to the browserCarries: The prebuilt React bundle and static assets No API call and no customer data yet.GET / -> index.html + JS chunks
2
Browser to Auth0Carries: Credentials, or a Google assertion Returns a signed token. No password ever reaches Litmus.{email, password} -> {access_token, id_token}
3
Browser to the load balancerCarries: Bearer token, target URL, adapter type, tier and any credentials the target endpoint needs.Bearer <jwt> + {target_url, adapter, tier, probes, creds}
4
Load balancer to FastAPICarries: The same request, now decrypted TLS ends at the ALB, so this hop is cleartext HTTP.same body, plus X-Request-ID, over HTTP :8000
5
FastAPI to RDSCarries: Tenant and user records, then the scan row Written at status pending, which returns a scan_id.INSERT scans{id, client_id, tier, status:'pending'}
6
FastAPI to the S3 configs prefixCarries: Scan YAML holding the target and its credentials Written over the gateway endpoint, deleted after the run.config.yaml{adapter, target.url, target.key, probes[]}
7
FastAPI to ECS RunTaskCarries: A control call only, carrying no customer data One task per scan. A deep scan launches da3lab-scan too.env{SCAN_ID, S3_BUCKET, CONFIG_S3_KEY, CALLBACK_URL}
8
FastAPI to RedisCarries: Queue message carrying scan_id and arguments A Celery worker takes it and polls ECS every fifteen seconds.{task:'monitor_scan_completion', args:[scan_id, arn]}
9
Scan task through the NAT to the customer AICarries: Adversarial prompts out, model responses back The largest and most sensitive flow in the platform.{messages:[{role:'user', content:'<attack prompt>'}]}
10
da3lab-scan through the NAT to BedrockCarries: Attack objective, jailbreak prompts, captured replies Deep scan only. Llama 3.3 70B attacks, Claude Haiku 4.5 judges.attacker{objective, feedback} -> judge{score, reason}
11
Scan task to the S3 report objectsCarries: report.json and report.html: findings and evidence Celery then parses them into one database row per finding.report.json{findings:[{severity, category, prompt, response}]}
12
Celery through the NAT to SES and the webhookCarries: Completion notice and a scan.completed payload Leaves the boundary for the customer's own systems.{event:'scan.completed', scan_id, counts, report_url}
What is stored, where, and where PHI can land8 stores, classified

Litmus is not a health system, but it captures verbatim model responses as evidence. If a customer points it at a clinical assistant, that evidence is the vector by which regulated data enters the platform. The orange halos mark every place that can happen.

StoreClassWhat it holdsWhat that implies
RDS PostgreSQLConfidential, PHI possibleIdentity and org records, scan metadata, hashed API keys, billing identifiers, and scan_findings rows that hold verbatim prompt and response evidence.If a customer points Litmus at a clinical chatbot, the captured evidence can contain PHI. This table is the most likely place for it to land.
S3, configs/ prefixSecretThe Checkmate YAML including the target endpoint and its credentials.Deleted after each run by delete_config_from_s3(). Worth an object-level log and a lifecycle rule so the deletion is evidenced, not just asserted.
S3, report objectsConfidential, PHI possiblereport.json and report.html per tier, with full attack evidence.Reachable by pre-signed URL and by no-auth share tokens. Both are bearer capabilities over the most sensitive artefact the platform holds.
ElastiCache RedisTransientQueue payloads, Celery results with a one-hour TTL, WebSocket to Playwright session mappings.Encrypted at rest and in transit. Nothing here is a system of record.
CloudWatch LogsPseudonymousStructured JSON with request_id and user_id on every line.No evidence bodies should be logged. If they are, this becomes a PHI store too, which is worth an explicit check.
Amazon BedrockPHI possible, in transit onlyAttack objectives, generated prompts and captured target responses, on Deep scans only.Nothing is persisted by configuration, but the payload crosses a service boundary. Model invocation logging must stay off, or be treated as a store.
Auth0Secret, outside AWSCredentials and the JWT signing private key.Deliberately outside the boundary. This is the reason no password ever reaches the platform.
StripeOut of scopePayment instruments.Card data never enters the AWS account, which keeps the platform outside PCI scope for cardholder data.

Encryption in transit and at rest12 entries, one exception

Green pills on the diagram mark encrypted hops. The single amber pill is the load balancer to application hop, which is cleartext by design inside the VPC.

WhereKindControl
Browser to ALBIn transitTLS 1.2 minimum, 1.3 preferred, ACM-managed certificate with automatic renewal.
ALB to FastAPIIn transitCleartext HTTP inside the VPC. Common and usually accepted, but it is the one hop where the request is readable to anything with packet access in the app subnet.
FastAPI and Celery to RDSIn transitTLS enforced by sslmode=require.
FastAPI and Celery to RedisIn transitElastiCache in-transit encryption enabled.
Everything to S3, ECR, SSMIn transitTLS to the endpoint. The bucket policy denies plain HTTP outright.
Everything outboundIn transitTLS to Bedrock, SES, Auth0, Stripe and customer endpoints, SigV4 signed where it is an AWS API.
S3At restSSE-KMS on every object.
RDS PostgreSQLAt restAES-256 storage encryption under a KMS key.
ElastiCache RedisAt restEncryption at rest enabled.
SSM Parameter Store and Secrets ManagerAt restSecureString and secret values under KMS. Injected into task environment at container start through the IAM task role.
JWT signingKey handlingRS256 asymmetric. The private key stays with Auth0; the platform only ever fetches public keys.
API keysKey handlingckm_ prefixed keys stored hashed in PostgreSQL. Plaintext is never persisted.
Well-Architected, six pillars on the diagram6 pillars, where each is decided

Each badge sits on the component where the pillar is actually decided, rather than on a checklist beside the drawing.

OE
Operational excellenceStructured JSON logs correlated by request_id and user_id, CloudWatch Insights queryable, a two minute deployment bake that fails fast on rolloutState, and Slack notification with PR and author. The open question is runbook coverage for a scan that hangs past the visibility timeout.
SEC
SecurityNo public IPs on any task, one ingress point, one egress point, secrets only from SSM and Secrets Manager, no static CI credentials, KMS everywhere, hashed API keys. The gaps are listed in the security overlay.
REL
Reliabilitytask_acks_late with prefetch of one, a dedicated notifications queue so long scan monitors cannot starve short tasks, ALB health checks deregistering unhealthy targets, and SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on schedule dispatch. Single-NAT and single-AZ exposure is worth confirming.
PERF
Performance efficiencyMoving Deep scan inference from CPU Ollama to Bedrock took a scan from three or four hours to about fifteen minutes. Basic and Deep run as parallel tasks rather than in sequence.
COST
Cost optimisationGateway and interface endpoints keep S3, ECR and SSM traffic off the NAT. Fargate tasks are ephemeral, so scan compute is only paid for while a scan runs. The unconfigured Bedrock endpoint is the one visible cost leak.
SUS
SustainabilityNothing idles for scan capacity. Tasks are created per scan and exit at completion, and the container images are shared across services rather than duplicated.

How a tenant is created for each customer

What actually happens between a signup form and a first scan, what exists per customer once it has, and where the boundary between two customers really sits. The short answer is that it sits in one place: the organisation identifier carried in the token and applied to every query.

How a tenant gets created10 steps, signup to first scan
1
Signup, or an invite from an existing tenantA Cloudflare Turnstile challenge is validated on the server before anything is created. Nothing is written until that passes.
2
Auth0 user and Auth0 Organization createdThe backend calls the Auth0 Management API through the NAT. Auth0 mints the organisation identifier that becomes the tenant's identity for the life of the account.
3
organizations and users rows written to RDSThe Auth0 identity is synced into the platform's own database. Social sign-in skips the signup form, so an onboarding step collects the company name afterwards and PATCHes it in.
4
The tenant identity enters every tokenFrom here the JWT carries sub, org_id, role, tier and permissions. Every later request resolves through AuthContext, and org_id is what scopes the query.
5
Stripe customer and subscription createdbilling_accounts and subscriptions rows link the tenant to its plan. The tier is what the entitlement check reads when a scan is requested.
6
An S3 prefix is reservedResults land under {client_id}/ in the shared bucket. The prefix is the isolation boundary for objects, enforced by application logic rather than by a bucket policy.
7
Quotas and platform defaults appliedScan quota and tier limits come from the subscription; PAIR iteration caps and worker settings come from the single global platform_config row shared by all tenants.
8
API keys issued on requestckm_ prefixed keys for CI and integrations, stored hashed. The key resolves to the same org_id as a session token would.
9
Users invited and roles assignedThe tenant administrator adds members through user management. Roles ride in the token as permissions rather than being looked up per request.
10
Every subsequent read and write is scopedScans, findings, reports, webhooks, schedules and prompt libraries all filter on the organisation. One control, applied consistently, is the whole isolation model.
What exists per tenant, and where12 objects
WhatWhere it livesIsolationWhat that means
Tenant identityAuth0 OrganizationShared Auth0 tenantThe identifier everything else keys to. Created first, and never changed.
Tenant recordRDS organizations rowShared database, shared schemaCompany name, metadata and the link to the Auth0 organisation.
UsersRDS users rows and Auth0 usersSharedMembership is an attribute of the user, not a separate tenant store.
Authorisationorg_id claim in the JWTIn the token, per requestResolved into AuthContext once per request and applied to every query.
Scans and findingsRDS scans and scan_findingsShared tables, filtered by org_idLogical isolation. A missing filter in one query is a cross-tenant read.
Reports and configsS3 under {client_id}/Shared bucket, per-tenant prefixPrefix separation enforced in code. The task role can reach the whole bucket.
Queue and cacheRedis, keyed by scan_idSharedPayloads are tenant data in transit through a shared broker.
BillingStripe customer and subscriptionStripe, plus identifiers in RDSTier drives entitlement, so a billing error is an access control error.
API keysRDS api_keys, hashedShared tableEach key resolves to one organisation. Revocation is a row update.
Encryption keysOne KMS key per storeShared across all tenantsNo per-tenant key today. This is the first thing an enterprise buyer asks about.
Platform settingsplatform_config, single global rowShared by every tenantPAIR caps, visibility timeout and worker counts are global, not per tenant.
LogsCloudWatch, correlated by request_id and user_idSharedTenant attribution exists but is not a separate stream per customer.
How to harden the model6 recommendations
  • This is a pooled model: one database, one bucket, one set of keys, with isolation enforced in application code. That is a normal and defensible choice at this stage, but it should be stated plainly in a security questionnaire rather than implied.
  • Because org_id in AuthContext is the only thing standing between tenants, it deserves a dedicated negative test suite that runs in CI: a cross-tenant scan_id, report_id, share token, webhook and S3 key, each expected to fail.
  • Postgres row-level security would move the isolation from every query to the database itself, so a forgotten filter fails closed instead of leaking. It is the highest-value change on this list.
  • An IAM condition on the S3 prefix, or a scan task role scoped to one client_id, would stop a compromised scan container from reading another tenant's reports. Today the task role can reach the whole bucket.
  • A per-tenant KMS key is the answer to the enterprise question about cryptographic separation, and it also gives a clean, provable deletion story: destroy the key and the data is unrecoverable regardless of what is left in backups.
  • For a customer who will not accept a pooled model at all, the fallback is a silo deployment in its own account. Price it deliberately rather than discovering the requirement in a negotiation.
Build

Security components still missing, and what they cost

The architecture is well built for what it does, but it is thin on the components that let you see, contain and prove. This is what I would add, in the order I would add it, with indicative monthly cost so the conversation is about sequencing rather than about whether. Roughly 950 to 2,700 US dollars a month for the paid route, though about two thirds of it has a credible free or open-source alternative, listed against each component, against a platform whose Bedrock and Fargate bill already moves with scan volume.

Phase 1, prove you can see6 components, about 250 to 700 US dollars a month

Nothing else works until you can detect and evidence. This is also the shortest path to passing a SOC 2 Type II observation window and a customer security review.

ComponentWhat it does and why it is needed hereMonthly, US dollarsFree or open-source route
CloudTrail organisation trailYou currently have no tamper-evident record of who did what in the account. Management events are free; the cost is the S3 storage and a data-event trail on the report bucket, which is the one place you want object-level history.5 to 25Free as it stands. Management events cost nothing; keep data events to the report prefix only and lifecycle the bucket to Glacier.
VPC flow logs to S3Every probe leaves through one NAT address. Without flow logs you cannot answer what a scan task actually connected to, which is the first question after any incident and the first question a customer asks when their WAF flags your traffic.15 to 70Generation is free. Deliver to S3 in Parquet with a 30 day lifecycle and query on demand with Athena, which is pennies. Never send them to CloudWatch.
Amazon GuardDutyContinuous threat detection against CloudTrail, DNS and flow logs, with Runtime Monitoring for Fargate. Your scan containers execute adversarial content and reach arbitrary internet hosts, which is exactly the workload you want behavioural detection on.70 to 250No true free equivalent for managed detection. Closest open-source route is Wazuh self-hosted on log data, plus EventBridge rules on high-signal CloudTrail events. Use the 30 day trial to measure real volume first.
AWS Security HubAggregates findings and scores you against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices and CIS benchmarks. It converts posture into a number you can show a customer and track over time.20 to 90Prowler, open source, run on a schedule in CI. It covers the CIS and AWS benchmarks and prints the same findings. ScoutSuite is the alternative.
AWS ConfigRecords resource configuration history and evaluates rules continuously. This is what proves a control was in place for the whole audit period rather than on the day the auditor looked.30 to 130Prowler on a schedule plus CloudTrail answers most of the audit question. CloudQuery snapshots resource state into Postgres if you want drift queries. Continuous history is the part you cannot replicate free.
AWS WAF on the load balancerThe ALB accepts 443 from anywhere with nothing in front of it. Managed rule groups plus rate limiting on the signup, login and scan-creation routes cost little and stop the noisy majority.25 to 90You already route through Cloudflare, so its managed rules and rate limiting are available on the free and Pro tiers. Combined with the slowapi limits already in the API, that covers the noisy majority at no AWS cost.
Phase 2, segment and contain6 components, about 400 to 1,100 US dollars a month

The architecture currently trusts itself. These changes limit what a compromise of the scan tier can reach, and close the two structural findings in the security overlay.

ComponentWhat it does and why it is needed hereMonthly, US dollarsFree or open-source route
Separate subnet and security group for scan tasksThe scan containers run attacker-shaped payloads and talk to untrusted endpoints. They currently share the private app subnet with the API and the Celery workers. Give them their own subnet, their own security group and no route to the data tier at all.0, design change onlyFree. This is a Terraform change, not a purchase.
Separate AWS accounts for staging and productionStaging and production resolve to the same load balancer today. Separate accounts under Organizations make a listener-rule mistake structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely, and give you a clean blast radius story.0 for accounts, 50 to 150 for the extra Config and loggingAccounts and Organizations are free. Control Tower itself is free; only the Config and logging it turns on costs anything.
Egress filtering for the scan tierRight now a compromised scan container can reach anything on the internet. An allowlist proxy, or AWS Network Firewall if you want the managed version, constrains outbound to the customer target and the AWS APIs you actually use.40 for a proxy on Fargate, 300 or more for Network FirewallSquid or Envoy on a small Fargate task, with an allowlist, is the free route and about a tenth of Network Firewall. mitmproxy is useful in development for seeing what a scan actually calls.
Second NAT gateway for the second availability zoneOne NAT gateway is one device on the path of every probe, every Bedrock call and every notification. A zone failure currently stops all scanning.35 plus data processingA NAT instance on a t4g.nano is a few dollars a month instead of thirty-five, at the cost of owning the patching. More endpoints also reduce how much depends on the NAT at all.
Bedrock interface endpointAlready identified in the cost overlay. Takes model traffic off the NAT, removes a per-gigabyte processing charge and keeps the inference call inside the AWS network.8 per AZ, usually net negative against the NAT charge it removesNot free, but it usually costs less than the NAT charge it removes. This is the one line item that pays for itself.
IAM Access Analyzer and Identity CenterFree. Finds resources shared outside the account and gives humans federated, MFA-backed access instead of long-lived users.0Already free. There is no paid tier to consider.
Certificate and key lifecycle7 components, about 0 to 60 US dollars a month, plus 400 a month only if you need a private CA

Certificates are the one control that fails silently and takes the whole platform down when it does. ACM renews the load balancer certificate automatically, but that renewal depends on a validation record held at a third-party DNS provider, and nothing in the architecture watches it.

ComponentWhat it does and why it is needed hereMonthly, US dollarsFree or open-source route
Certificate inventory and expiry alertingACM auto-renews, but only while the validation CNAME survives in the DNS zone. If that record is edited or removed, renewal fails quietly and you discover it when the site stops loading. A Config rule for expiry plus an EventBridge rule on ACM renewal failure turns a silent outage into a ticket.0 to 10EventBridge plus SNS is free. If you want it outside AWS, a scheduled job running openssl s_client against both hostnames does the same in ten lines.
DNS zone and registrar lockdownWhoever can edit the DNS records can obtain a valid certificate for your domain. The zone lives at a third-party provider today and deserves the same MFA, access review and registrar lock as the AWS account itself. Enable DNSSEC if the provider supports it.0, process and access controlFree. MFA, registrar lock and an access review are process, not product.
Certificate transparency monitoringEvery publicly trusted certificate is logged. Watching those logs for your two domains is how you find out somebody else has issued a certificate for them, which is otherwise undetectable from inside your account.0 to 25Free. crt.sh has a public API, Cert Spotter has a free tier, and certstream gives a live feed if you want alerting rather than polling.
TLS policy enforced as codeThe load balancer policy is right today. A Config rule that fails when the listener drops below TLS 1.2 is what keeps it right after the next change, and it is evidence for the audit rather than a screenshot.included in Config abovetestssl.sh or sslyze in CI, both open source, will fail a build on a weak policy without Config.
mTLS on the scan callback pathThe progress callback from a scan container to the API is authenticated by a shared bearer token injected into every task. A client certificate binds that call to a specific workload identity instead, so a leaked token is no longer sufficient on its own.0 with a self-managed trust storeFree with a self-managed trust store on the load balancer. The certificates can come from step-ca below.
Private CA, only if internal TLS is requiredAWS Private CA is the clean answer for encrypting the load balancer to application hop and issuing workload certificates. It is also four hundred dollars a month before a single certificate is issued, so treat it as a Phase 3 decision driven by a customer requirement, not a default.400, plus per-certificate chargesstep-ca from Smallstep, or cfssl, both open source and self-hosted. This is the four hundred dollar line item with the strongest free substitute.
Container image signingSigning images and verifying the signature at deployment closes the gap between the pipeline that built an artefact and the cluster that runs it. Near free, and it maps directly to the software supply chain questions a medtech customer will ask.0 to 15Sigstore cosign, keyless with OIDC. Free, and it is what most of the ecosystem has standardised on.
Phase 3, investigate, survive and prove content6 components, about 300 to 900 US dollars a month, or considerably more with a vendor SIEM

Detection without a place to search it is a dashboard nobody opens. This phase also covers recovery and the PHI question the data overlay raises.

ComponentWhat it does and why it is needed hereMonthly, US dollarsFree or open-source route
SIEM, starting with Security Lake and AthenaNormalises CloudTrail, flow logs, GuardDuty and application logs into one queryable store in OCSF format. At your size this is a tenth of the cost of a vendor SIEM and answers the same audit question. Move to a vendor product when you have someone whose job is to watch it.80 to 250, against 500 to 3,000 for a vendor SIEMS3 plus Athena is already close to free at your volume. Fully open source alternatives are Matano for an OCSF lake, Wazuh for detection, or Grafana with Loki for application logs.
Amazon Macie on the report bucketThe data overlay says report objects can contain PHI. Macie is how you find out whether they actually do, rather than assuming. Run it as a sampling job on new objects, not a full scan.50 to 200 depending on sample rateMicrosoft Presidio, open source, run in a Lambda over new objects. It is genuinely good at PHI and PII detection and it is the better fit for evidence text than a managed scanner.
Amazon Inspector for ECR imagesContinuous vulnerability scanning of the three container images. Cheap, and it is the control a medtech customer will ask about by name because it maps to their own SBOM obligation.20 to 70Trivy or Grype in CI, with Syft for the SBOM and Dependency-Track to watch it over time. Free, and a better answer for a medtech customer asking about SBOM than Inspector alone.
Multi-AZ RDS with cross-region snapshot copyA single-AZ database is a single point of loss for every finding you have ever produced. Multi-AZ roughly doubles the instance cost; the cross-region copy is what makes a regional outage survivable.roughly the current RDS instance cost again, plus 10 to 40 for the copiesNo free substitute for the availability half. Single-AZ with point-in-time recovery, pgBackRest to S3 and a written recovery objective is the honest cheaper position, as long as it is written down.
AWS Backup with an immutable vault in a second accountBackups in the same account as the thing they protect do not survive an account compromise. A vault with lock in a separate account is the control that makes ransomware recoverable.20 to 80Cross-account S3 replication with Object Lock gives you most of it free, for the objects. The database still needs somewhere to put its dumps.
S3 versioning and lifecycle on the report bucketVersioning protects against accidental or malicious deletion; lifecycle rules are how the retention schedule is actually enforced rather than merely written down.5 to 30Free. Configuration only.
What has no free substitute4 items worth actually budgeting for
no
Managed threat detectionGuardDuty correlates CloudTrail, DNS and flow data with maintained threat intelligence, and adds runtime monitoring inside a Fargate task. Wazuh gets you log-based detection; it does not get you the intelligence feed or the runtime hooks. Budget for this one.
no
Availability of the data tierMulti-AZ RDS and a second NAT gateway are availability, and availability is not something open source can donate. The free position is single-AZ with point-in-time recovery and a recovery objective you have written down and tested.
no
Continuous configuration historyProwler on a schedule tells you the state today. AWS Config tells an auditor what the state was on every day of the observation window. That difference is what you are paying for, and it only matters once you are in a SOC 2 window.
no
Everything elseHas a credible free or open-source route, listed against each component. Roughly two thirds of the programme can start at zero cost, which changes the conversation from budget approval to engineering time.
What these numbers assume5 notes
  • Figures are AWS list price in us-east-1, rounded to indicative monthly ranges, and assume a single region, roughly fifty to two hundred scans a day, under a terabyte of monthly egress and a small team. They are order-of-magnitude planning numbers, not a quote.
  • Costs that scale with volume, particularly GuardDuty, flow logs, Macie and the SIEM store, will move with scan volume rather than with customer count. Model them per scan, not per tenant.
  • The Bedrock interface endpoint and the S3 lifecycle rules both reduce spend. They are the two items on this list that pay for themselves.
  • Phase 1 and Phase 2 together are roughly the cost of a single mid-size Fargate service running continuously. Set against one enterprise medtech deal, the whole programme is noise; set against a failed security review, it is the cheapest insurance on the list.
  • Nothing here is a substitute for the four open items in the security overlay. Tooling detects; those are design decisions that have to be made regardless of what you buy.
Register

Vendors, controllers and subprocessors

Every third party the three diagrams touch, and what each one actually sees. This is the list a customer's privacy team will ask for, and the list that has to appear in a data processing agreement before the first regulated customer signs.

In the data path8 parties that see customer data
PartyRoleWhat it processesWhereWhat that means
Amazon Web ServicesSubprocessor, infrastructureEverything the platform holds: tenant records, scan configuration including target credentials, findings and their verbatim evidence, reports, queue payloads, logs and keys.us-east-1The controller of record for the underlying compute, storage and key material. A single-region deployment, which simplifies the data residency answer but concentrates it.
Amazon BedrockSubprocessor, model inferenceDeep scans only: the attack objective, every generated jailbreak prompt and the target's captured responses, sent for scoring.us-east-1, us-west-2, us-east-2Cross-region inference profiles mean a prompt may be processed outside us-east-1. That is a data residency commitment the platform cannot make on a single-region basis, and it should be stated in the customer agreement rather than discovered.

A third party fronting the production hostname needs a named role, a contract and a security review, or it needs removing from the chain.
Amazon SESSubprocessor, transactional emailRecipient address and scan completion metadata. No findings or evidence in the message body.us-east-1Part of the AWS agreement, but worth listing separately because it is the only path by which platform data reaches a mailbox outside the customer's control.

PartyRoleWhat it processesWhereWhat that means
