Schedule

How long to keep each thing

A suggested retention schedule for every store in the diagrams: what it holds, where it lives, how long to keep it and which obligation sets the clock. Retention is the control that turns a data map into a defensible position, and it is usually the first thing a customer's privacy team asks for. These are engineering suggestions to take to counsel, not legal advice, and the periods need confirming against your own contracts and jurisdictions.

Suggested retention schedule13 categories
DataWhereSuggested periodDriverWhy that number
Scan findings and their evidenceRDS scan_findings12 months by default, customer-selectable at 30, 90 or 365 daysGDPR Art. 5(1)(e) storage limitation; customer DPAThis is the highest-sensitivity store in the platform and the one most likely to hold PHI. The defensible default is the shortest period that still lets a customer show remediation progress between scans.
Report objects, JSON and HTMLS3 report prefixSame clock as the findings, enforced by an S3 lifecycle ruleGDPR Art. 5(1)(e); SOC 2 CC6Two stores holding the same evidence must expire together. A lifecycle rule is the control; the application deleting rows is not enough.
Scan configuration holding target credentialsS3 configs prefixDeleted at scan completion, with a 24-hour lifecycle rule as a backstopNo regulation requires retention; least privilegeThe application already deletes these. Add the lifecycle rule so a crashed scan cannot leave a credential behind, and enable object-level logging so deletion is evidenced rather than asserted.
Queue payloads and task resultsElastiCache RedisOne hour, already enforced by TTLNoneNo change needed. Worth stating explicitly in the DPA because customers ask what the cache holds.
Application logsCloudWatch Logs90 days hot, then export to S3 for 12 monthsSOC 2 audit period; ISO 27001 A.8.15Twelve months covers a full SOC 2 observation window. Keep evidence bodies out of these logs, or this becomes a second PHI store with a longer clock than the first.
Load balancer and CDN access logsS330 to 90 days until the token-in-URL issue is closed, then 12 monthsSOC 2; PCI DSS 10.5.1 if ever in scopeThese logs currently capture the progress-stream access token in the query string. Until that is fixed, a long retention on access logs is a credential store with a twelve-month life.
Authentication and administrative audit eventsRDS, exported to S312 months minimum; 6 years where you act for a HIPAA covered entity45 CFR 164.316(b)(2); SOC 2 CC7Who ran which scan, who issued or revoked a key, who changed platform config. Separate this from application logs so it can outlive them without dragging evidence along.
Tenant and user account recordsRDSLife of contract, then deleted within 30 days of terminationGDPR Art. 17; customer DPAPublish the deletion window as a commitment. A named number is worth more in a security review than a paragraph of intent.
Billing and invoice recordsStripe, and identifiers in RDS7 years, held by StripeStatutory tax and accounting retentionStripe is an independent controller for this, so its clock is longer than yours and that is correct. Keep only the identifiers on your side.
Database backups and snapshotsRDS automated backups35 days maximum point-in-time recoveryGDPR Art. 17 erasure caveatAn erasure request cannot reach a snapshot. State in the DPA that deletion completes when the backup window rolls, and keep that window short enough to be a credible answer.
Model invocation logsAmazon BedrockKeep disabledGDPR; HIPAA if PHI is presentIf model invocation logging is ever switched on, Bedrock stops being a transit path and becomes a store holding target prompts and responses, in a region that may not be your own.
Security incident and investigation recordsYour own systems6 years45 CFR 164.316(b)(2); ISO 27001 A.5.28The longest clock in the register, and the one most often forgotten because it lives outside the product.
The customer's copy of a reportCustomer-sideDevice design life plus 2 years, for medical device customers21 CFR 820.180(b) and 820.30 design history fileThis is the important mismatch. A device manufacturer may need to retain security testing evidence far longer than you should hold it. Solve that with a durable export they own, not by extending your own retention.
MT

Multi-tenant protection, as-is and to-be

Litmus runs a pooled model, so isolation is something the application does on every query rather than something the infrastructure guarantees. This sets out what holds today and what would make it structural.

What multi-tenancy means, in plain wordsthe idea itself, before the platform

Worth setting out on its own, because as-is and to-be only make sense once the question is clear.

1
What multi-tenancy actually meansOne copy of the software, one set of databases, many customers. It is the reason a SaaS product can charge a hundred pounds a month instead of ten thousand: everybody shares the same machines, and something has to keep their data apart. The alternative, one deployment per customer, is what enterprise software used to be, and it is why it cost what it cost.
2
Why it is a security question, not an architecture oneNothing physical separates two customers in a pooled system. What separates them is a decision made on every single request: this row belongs to that customer, so do not return it. Get it right ten thousand times and nobody notices. Get it wrong once and you have handed one customer another customer’s data, which is the one incident a SaaS company rarely survives intact.
3
The only question worth askingNot "are we multi-tenant", but "what happens the day someone forgets". If the answer is a leak, the boundary lives in code and depends on people being careful. If the answer is an empty result, an access denied, or a decryption failure, the boundary lives in the platform. Everything on this page is about moving from the first answer to the second.
4
As-is means what is true todayNot what the design intends, and not what the policy says. What the running system would actually do if a query shipped without a filter this afternoon. That is the version worth writing down, because it is the version a customer’s security team will find.
5
To-be means what would make it structuralOrdered by value for effort, not by ambition. Most of the list is configuration rather than rearchitecture, and the two or three items at the top change the failure mode rather than adding a feature.
What it means herethe same idea, applied to this platform
L
What this means for Litmus specificallyLitmus is pooled, and the boundary is the org_id claim in the Auth0 token applied to every query in application code. The unusual part is what sits behind that boundary: not just account records, but the verbatim prompts and model replies captured as evidence, which is the most sensitive artefact the platform holds and the one most likely to contain regulated data. A cross-tenant read here is not a leaked invoice, it is one customer reading another customer’s AI failures.
L
And what makes it harder than the usual caseTwo components sit on both sides of the line. FastAPI arranges work and also serves findings and report links. One S3 bucket holds scan configs with target credentials and reports with evidence, one prefix apart, and the scan task role reaches both. So the answer to "what protects tenant A from tenant B" is not one control, it is a filter, a prefix and a shared role, all applied by code.
The isolation ladderfive levels, and what each one costs

Every multi-tenant decision is a choice of level on the same ladder. Naming the level you are on is more useful than arguing about whether you are isolated.

L0
Shared, separated by a value in application codeOne database, one bucket, one cache, one key. Every query carries a tenant identifier and the application is trusted to apply it. Cheapest to run and cheapest to get wrong: a single missing WHERE clause is a cross-tenant read, and nothing below the application would stop it. This is where both platforms sit today.
L1
Shared, separated by a value the platform enforcesSame infrastructure, but the separation moves out of application code and into something that fails closed. Row-level security in Postgres, an IAM condition on the S3 prefix, a client wrapper that refuses an unnamespaced Redis key. Almost no extra cost, and it converts the failure mode from silent leak to empty result. This is the level worth reaching for both platforms.
L2
Shared infrastructure, separate namespaces and keysOne instance, but a schema per tenant, a bucket prefix with its own key, a per-tenant KMS data key. Costs a key and some operational surface per tenant. Buys crypto-shredding for erasure and a clean story for a customer who asks about cryptographic separation, without running a fleet.
L3
Separate instances for the tenants who pay for themA dedicated database, bucket, cache or proxy service for one customer. Real money and real operational load per tenant, so it belongs in a premium tier rather than as a default. Worth designing for now so that the first customer who demands it is a configuration change rather than a rebuild.
L4
Separate AWS accountsThe only level where a mistake in one tenant cannot reach another by construction. Accounts are free; the cost is the pipeline, the logging and the operational discipline to run more than one. For most platforms the right first use of this level is separating staging from production, not separating customers.
Store by store, as-is and to-benine stores, with the control that enforces each

The general answer is level 1: keep the shared infrastructure and move the separation out of application code into something that fails closed. Separate databases and buckets appear only where a customer is paying for them.

As-is todayTo-beWhat enforces it
RDS PostgreSQLOne instance, shared tables, isolation by an org_id filter written into every query by hand.Row-level security policies on organizations, users, scans, scan_findings, api_keys and subscriptions, with the org set per connection from AuthContext. Optionally a schema per tenant for the largest accounts, and a dedicated instance only where a customer contracts for one.A Postgres policy, not a code review. A forgotten filter returns zero rows instead of somebody else’s findings.
S3 report objectsOne bucket, one {client_id}/ prefix per tenant, applied by the application. The scan task role can read the whole bucket.An IAM condition restricting s3:prefix to the caller’s own client_id, carried as a session tag on the task role. A per-tenant bucket only for a customer who needs their own bucket policy or their own CMK.An IAM policy condition plus a session tag. Turns the prefix from a convention into a boundary.
S3 configs prefixSame bucket as the reports. Holds the target endpoint and its credentials until the scan deletes it.A separate bucket from the reports, because the two have different sensitivities and different clocks. A 24 hour lifecycle rule as a backstop, and object-level logging so deletion is evidenced.Bucket separation, lifecycle rule, CloudTrail data events on the prefix.
ElastiCache RedisOne cluster, one keyspace, shared by every tenant and by both queues.Tenant-prefixed keys enforced by a thin client wrapper that refuses an unnamespaced key, and separate logical databases for the queue and the cache. A dedicated cluster only in a premium tier.A library that fails the call, plus a lint rule. Cheap and effective.
KMS keysOne key per store, shared by every tenant.A per-tenant data key for the report prefix, bound with an encryption context carrying client_id, so a key policy can require the context to match. Erasure then becomes deleting one key.Encryption context condition in the key policy. It also gives you crypto-shredding for free.
Scan computeEphemeral Fargate tasks, but every tenant’s scan runs under the same IAM task role, which also grants RunTask and SES send.A scoped role assumed per scan with session tags for client_id and scan_id, holding only what a scan needs: read its own config, write its own report prefix, invoke Bedrock. RunTask and SES move to the orchestrator role.AssumeRole with session tags, plus policy conditions on those tags.
NetworkScan tasks share the private app subnet with the API and the Celery workers, and reach the internet through the shared NAT.A dedicated subnet and security group for the scan tier, with no route to the data tier at all, and an egress allowlist so a compromised scan container cannot reach arbitrary hosts.Route table and security group. It is a Terraform change, not a purchase.
Report deliveryPre-signed URLs and no-auth share tokens, both bearer capabilities over the most sensitive artefact the platform holds.Short-lived links, one-time share tokens bound to a recipient, and object-level logging on the report prefix so a read is a recorded event.Signed URL TTL, a token table, and CloudTrail data events.
LogsShared CloudWatch log groups, correlated by request_id and user_id.The same groups, plus an enforced rule that no evidence body is ever logged, checked in CI rather than asserted in a policy. Per-tenant log stream naming so a support query can be scoped.A CI check on the logging calls. It is the cheapest control on this table.
As-iswhat protects one tenant from another today

Six mechanisms carry the whole guarantee. Five of them are application code, which is the point worth being honest about.

1
One deployment, every customerThe Orchestrator, one RDS instance, one Redis cluster, one S3 bucket and one KMS key per store serve everybody. Signing up creates records, never infrastructure.
2
org_id in the token is the whole boundaryAuth0 issues a JWT carrying org_id. The API resolves it into an AuthContext once per request, and every query filters on it. A forgotten filter is a cross-tenant read, and nothing below the application layer would stop it.
3
S3 separates by prefix, enforced in codeReports and scan configs sit under a {client_id}/ prefix. The prefix is the isolation boundary and it is applied by the application, not by a bucket policy, and the scan task role can reach the whole bucket.
4
One shared task role for every scanAU8 is a single IAM task role used by every tenant’s scan, and it grants RunTask and SES send alongside S3 and Bedrock. A scan container holds permissions it has no reason to hold.
5
Report links are bearer capabilitiesPre-signed URLs and no-auth share tokens reach the most sensitive artefact the platform holds. Whoever has the link has the report, tenant or not.
6
One global config rowPAIR caps, visibility timeout and worker counts come from a single platform_config row, so one tenant’s tuning is everyone’s tuning.
To-besix changes, in the order I would make them

Ordered by value for effort. The first two turn conventions into controls and neither requires a rewrite.

1
Row-level security in PostgresA forgotten org_id filter should fail closed at the database rather than return another tenant’s rows. This is the single highest-value change on the list and it is a migration, not a rewrite.
2
An IAM condition on the S3 prefixScope the scan task role to s3:prefix matching its own client_id. Turns the prefix from a convention into a control, and it is a policy change with no application impact.
3
Separate subnet and security group for scan tasksThe containers that run attacker payloads currently share the private app subnet with the API and the workers. Give them their own subnet, their own group and no route to the data tier.
4
Tenant isolation tests in CIA test that creates two orgs, writes data as one and asserts the other cannot read it, on every merge. It is the only thing that keeps the guarantee true after the next refactor.
5
Per-tenant CMK where a customer asksNot a default. It costs real money per key and only matters to customers who ask for cryptographic separation. Worth having a written answer ready rather than a key policy.
6
Expiring share links, and object-level loggingBound the share token, log object reads on the report prefix, and the bearer problem becomes an auditable one.
Planes

Data, control and management planes

Every component in the architecture does one of four jobs. Which one it does decides what a compromise of it costs you, and it is the fastest way to answer a reviewer who asks what touches customer content.

Planes diagramevery component sorted into one of four planes
In plain words, with no jargonwhat a plane is, and why anyone bothered inventing the idea

Think of a restaurant. Everything that happens there falls into one of four jobs, and the same four jobs turn up in every piece of software once it is big enough to matter.

1
The food going to the table is the data planeA plate leaves the kitchen and arrives in front of a customer. That is the thing the customer came for, and it is the thing that can be dropped, poisoned or stolen. In software the plate is the customer’s actual data, and the data plane is every hand it passes through on the way.
2
The order book is the control planeSomebody takes the order, checks the customer is allowed to have it, tells the kitchen what to make, and writes down what was served. Nobody eats the order book. But if you change it, every plate after that is wrong, and if you tear pages out, nobody can prove what happened. That is the control plane: it decides and it records.
3
The builders and the cameras are the management planeSomeone built the kitchen, hired the cooks, and put up the cameras. They are not there at dinner service, but they decided what the kitchen can do and whether anyone would notice a problem. Change the kitchen and you have changed every meal, without ever touching a plate.
4
The farm is outside the boundaryThe vegetables come from a farm you do not own. You can choose the farm, read its certificate and stop buying from it, but you cannot walk into its fields and fix things. All you have is the contract.
?
Why anyone bothered making this distinctionBecause when something goes wrong, the first question is what was actually lost, and the answer is different for each plane. Lose the data plane and someone read one customer’s content. Lose the control plane and someone changed the rules for everybody, and may have erased the proof. Lose the management plane and someone changed what is running, so the other two were never safe to begin with. One incident, three completely different phone calls.
What the four planes meanthe question each one answers, and what a compromise of it costs

A plane is a job, not a place. All four usually run in the same account, often on the same subnet, so the split is only visible if the drawing says so. The reason to draw it is that each plane fails differently.

DP
Data plane, on the request pathThe path a customer request actually travels, and the only place customer content exists in the clear. It answers: what touches the content. A compromise here exposes the content itself, one request at a time or in bulk, and it is the plane a customer means when they ask who can read their prompts.
CP
Control plane, decides and recordsAuthenticates the caller, resolves the tenant, decides what is allowed, and writes the record of what happened. It answers: who decided, and on what basis. A compromise here does not read content directly. It does something worse: it changes what the data plane is willing to do, and it can rewrite or suppress the evidence that it did.
MP
Management plane, builds and watchesPipelines, images, roles, logs, detection and human access. It answers: what is running, who put it there, and who would notice. A compromise here is the supply chain answer: change the artifact and you own both other planes, or blind the detection and own them quietly.
OB
Outside the boundary, governed by contractThird parties that hold or receive something you care about. It answers: what is not yours to control. The control is a contract and a review, not a security group, and the honest position on a diagram is to draw them outside and say so.
The same four jobs, in Litmuswhat the plate, the order book and the cameras actually are here
1
The plate is a prompt and a model’s answerLitmus sends attack prompts to a customer’s own AI and keeps what it says back, word for word, as evidence. That evidence is the plate. It travels from the scan task, out through the NAT gateway, to the customer’s model and back, and it ends up in the findings table and in the report file. Those are the only places it exists.
2
The order book is who may scan, and what happenedThe Orchestrator checks who is asking, whether their plan allows a deep scan, writes down that the scan exists, and hands the scan task a config file telling it what to attack. It never sends an attack prompt itself. It also holds the record of every finding, which is the part a customer will ask about in an audit.
3
The builders are the pipeline, the cameras are mostly not installed yetGitHub Actions builds the containers and pushes them, using a temporary AWS identity rather than a stored password, which is the good half. The cameras are the missing half: CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config and Security Hub are on the list to add, not running today. So Litmus can build safely but would struggle to notice a problem.
4
The farms are Auth0, Stripe and the customer’s own AIAuth0 keeps the passwords so Litmus never has to. Stripe keeps the card numbers for the same reason. The customer’s AI endpoint is the thing being tested, and it belongs to the customer. All three are outside the fence on purpose.
Protecting each plane, as-is and to-befour planes, and what changes

The plane split is only useful if it changes what you do. This is what protecting each one looks like today and what it would look like next.

PlaneAs-is todayTo-beWhat it buys you
Data planeEphemeral tasks with no public IP, one shared NAT, one shared task role, evidence written to shared RDS and S3, and reports reachable by bearer link.Dedicated subnet and security group, egress allowlist, a scoped per-scan role, per-tenant key on the report prefix, short-lived links with object-level logging, and Macie sampling the bucket so you know whether PHI is actually present rather than assuming.Everything a compromise of a scan container could reach shrinks to that scan.
Control planeFastAPI and Celery on shared infrastructure. org_id in the token is the only boundary. API keys are hashed. One global platform_config row.Row-level security so the boundary survives a forgotten filter, and a split between the orchestration API and the results API so the control plane stops handling customer content. Per-tenant configuration instead of one global row. Administrative actions written to an append-only trail.The control plane stops being able to read content at all, which is what makes the plane split true rather than aspirational.
Management planeGitHub Actions with OIDC and no static keys, images in ECR, logs in CloudWatch. No CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config or Security Hub.Enable all four, sign images with cosign and verify at deploy, add permission boundaries and service control policies, and separate staging from production into their own accounts.The account gains a tamper-evident record of who changed what, which is the precondition for every other claim on this page.
Outside the boundaryAuth0 holds credentials, Stripe holds payment instruments, the customer’s AI endpoint receives the probes.A published sub-processor list with a change notification commitment, a provider retention statement, and a DPA that names each party and what it sees.The contractual half of the control, which is the only half available at this level.
What this means for Litmustwo components sit in two planes at once, and that is the finding
1
The scan tasks are the whole data planecheckmate-scan and da3lab-scan are the only components that generate adversarial traffic and receive a customer model’s reply. They are ephemeral, created per scan and destroyed at exit, so the data plane has no standing existence between scans. That is a genuinely strong position, and it is worth saying out loud in a questionnaire.
2
FastAPI sits in both planesIt arranges work: authenticate, check tier, write the scan row, stage the config, call RunTask, poll. That is control plane. It also returns findings and mints pre-signed report links, which is customer content. That is data plane. So "the API is the control plane" is not quite true, and a reviewer who reads the results API carefully will find that themselves.
3
S3 sits in both planes tooOne bucket holds the configs prefix, which is control plane and carries the target credentials, and the report objects, which are data plane and carry verbatim evidence. Same bucket, same key, one prefix apart, and the scan task role can reach both.
4
The management plane is the thin oneGitHub Actions with OIDC and no static keys is good. What is missing is the watching half: CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config and Security Hub are all on the build list rather than in the account, so today the management plane can build but it cannot notice.
5
Auth0 and Stripe are outside on purposeNo password and no card number ever reaches the AWS account, which keeps two whole categories of breach outside the boundary. The customer’s own AI endpoint is outside too, and it is the one the data plane deliberately reaches.
Read

What these views are showing

A written walkthrough of each view: what it is for, how the thing it describes actually works step by step, and what I would change. Download it as Word or PDF if you want to circulate it without the diagrams.

every section below, in one document
OV-1, the operational conceptwhat a scan is, told once, end to end

What it is showing

OV-1 answers one question: what happens when a customer runs a scan, and which boundaries that crosses. It is deliberately the only view with no AWS detail on it, because the first thing a reviewer needs is the shape of the thing.

Three zones. The customer, who owns the AI being tested. Litmus, which runs in one AWS account. And the AI endpoint itself, which belongs to the customer and is drawn separately because it is the only thing that receives an attack.

How it works, step by step

  1. The team signs in through Auth0 and names a target: the endpoint, the adapter type and the tier.
  2. The request crosses into AWS over TLS carrying a signed token that names the user, the organization and their permissions.
  3. The Orchestrator records the scan, stages a config file into S3 and calls ECS RunTask. No customer data is in that call.
  4. Checkmate, the basic scan, fires static and fuzzing probes at the target through the NAT gateway, from one fixed address.
  5. If the customer chose the deep tier, DA3Lab starts alongside it and runs an attacker and judge loop on Bedrock. It is parallel, not sequential.
  6. Responses come back, are scored, and become findings carrying severity, category and the verbatim prompt and reply as evidence.
  7. Findings, a time-limited report link, an email and a webhook go back to the customer.
  8. The team triages, remediates and re-scans, on demand or on a schedule.

How to improve it

  • Only steps 4a and 4b leave the trust boundary, and both carry the customer’s own prompts and their model’s replies. Saying that on the diagram, as it does now, pre-empts the first question in every security review.
  • The 510(k)-style question a regulated buyer asks next is what happens to the evidence. A retention line on OV-1 pointing at the retention view would close that loop.
  • The narration transcript is gone, so the only remaining risk of drift is between OV-1 and the reference architecture. Keeping the step numbers identical across both is what prevents it.
SV-1, the reference architecturethe same scan, as deployed

What it is showing

The reference architecture is the deployment view: one AWS account, one region, a VPC with three subnet tiers, and eight overlays that answer a different question over the same drawing. It is the view an auditor reads.

The overlays exist so that data classification, protocols, encryption, lifecycle, IAM, keys, SOC 2 and Well-Architected are all answered from one picture rather than eight, which is what stops them contradicting each other.

How it works, step by step

  1. Traffic arrives at CloudFront and Amplify for the front end, and at the Application Load Balancer for the API.
  2. FastAPI on Fargate authenticates, checks tier and permissions, and writes the scan row.
  3. The config is staged into the S3 configs prefix, carrying the target credentials.
  4. ECS RunTask launches one or two scan tasks in the private app subnet, with no public IP.
  5. The tasks reach the customer target and, for deep scans, Bedrock, through the single NAT gateway.
  6. Celery polls ECS, parses the report, and writes findings into RDS.
  7. Notifications go out through SES and a webhook, and the report is served by a pre-signed S3 link.

How to improve it

  • Three structural gaps show on the drawing itself: no separate subnet or security group for the scan tier, one shared IAM task role, and no VPC endpoint for Bedrock.
  • The account has no tamper-evident record. CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config and Security Hub are all on the build list rather than in the account, which is the first phase of the security build for a reason.
  • Single NAT and single AZ are the availability exposure. A second NAT in a second AZ, and Multi-AZ RDS, are the two changes that turn a zone failure from an outage into a degradation.
OV-2, the data flow sequencewhat each hop actually carries

What it is showing

The data flow view is the one that matters for a threat model. It is not the call order that matters, it is the payload on each hop and which side of a boundary it ends on.

Twelve hops, each annotated with the actual fields it carries, which is what lets someone answer where PHI could land without guessing.

How it works, step by step

  1. The browser fetches a prebuilt bundle. No customer data yet.
  2. Credentials go to Auth0 and a token comes back. No password reaches Litmus.
  3. The scan request reaches the load balancer carrying the bearer token, the target URL, the adapter and any target credentials.
  4. The same request, now decrypted, moves from the ALB to FastAPI over plain HTTP inside the VPC.
  5. FastAPI writes the tenant and scan rows to RDS.
  6. The config YAML, with the target credentials in it, is written to the S3 configs prefix.
  7. ECS RunTask is called with no customer data, only identifiers and a callback URL.
  8. A Celery job is queued carrying the scan_id.
  9. The scan task sends adversarial prompts out through the NAT and receives model output back.
  10. For deep scans, the attack objective and the captured reply go to Bedrock for scoring.
  11. The report is written to S3 and parsed into findings.
  12. A completion notice and a webhook payload leave through the NAT.

How to improve it

  • Steps 9, 10 and 12 are the only ones that leave the trust boundary, and each carries customer prompts, customer model output, or the findings drawn from them. That sentence is the whole data-residency answer.
  • The hop from the ALB to FastAPI is cleartext inside the VPC. It is a common and defensible choice, but it is worth stating rather than leaving to be discovered.
  • The pre-signed report link and the no-auth share token are both bearer capabilities over the most sensitive artefact the platform holds. Bounding and logging them is the highest-value change in this view.
Call flow, the panel under OV-1the same steps, as a timeline

What it is showing

OV-1 shows where things sit. The call flow panel underneath it shows when they happen. Every component gets a lane, time runs downward, and each numbered row is one hop between two lanes.

The numbers are identical to OV-1 on purpose, so the two can be read side by side without translation.

How it works, step by step

  1. The team signs in at Auth0 and the token comes back.
  2. The web app crosses into AWS with that token.
  3. The Orchestrator launches the basic scan task.
  4. Checkmate probes the customer target, marked 4a.
  5. DA3Lab runs its attacker and judge loop on Bedrock, marked 4b, at the same time.
  6. Scored responses come back to the Orchestrator.
  7. The result is delivered to the team.
  8. The team closes the loop by re-scanning.

How to improve it

  • The two unnumbered rows at the bottom carry the facts that make 4a and 4b parallel: the deep scan launches a second task, and that task probes the same target. Those could be numbered if you would rather every row have an index.
  • A time axis with rough durations, five to thirty minutes for the basic scan and about fifteen for the deep loop, would turn this from an ordering diagram into a latency one.
Tenancy, how a customer is createdten steps, twelve objects, six fixes

What it is showing

What actually happens between a signup form and a first scan, what exists per customer once it has, and where the boundary between two customers really sits.

The short answer is that it sits in one place: the organisation identifier carried in the token and applied to every query. That is a normal choice for a platform at this stage, and it is worth being explicit rather than implying more separation than exists.

How it works, step by step

  1. A signup creates an Auth0 Organization, which becomes the tenant identity for the life of the account.
  2. Rows are written in organizations and users.
  3. A Stripe customer and subscription are created.
  4. A key prefix is reserved in the shared S3 bucket.
  5. The token issued from then on carries org_id, role, tier and permissions.
  6. Every API request resolves that token into an AuthContext once, and every query filters on it.
  7. Scans, findings and reports are written under the same identifier.

How to improve it

  • Row-level security in Postgres is the single highest-value change: it turns a forgotten filter from a cross-tenant read into an empty result set.
  • An IAM condition on the S3 prefix turns the {client_id}/ convention into a control.
  • Tenant isolation tests in CI are what keep both true after the next refactor.
Multi-tenant protection, as-is and to-besix mechanisms, six changes

What it is showing

The same subject as the tenancy view, stated as a before and after so it can be handed to an engineer or a buyer without interpretation.

As-is lists the six mechanisms that carry the whole guarantee today. Five of the six are application code, and that is the sentence a reviewer needs to hear from you rather than discover on their own.

How to improve it

  • The order matters more than the list. Row-level security and the S3 prefix condition come first because neither needs a rewrite and both change the failure mode from silent to safe.
  • A separate subnet and security group for the scan tier is the next one, because the containers running attacker payloads currently share a subnet with the API.
  • Per-tenant keys sit last deliberately. They cost real money per key and only matter to customers who ask for cryptographic separation, so a written answer is worth more than a key policy.
Planes, data, control and managementwhy the distinction earns its place

What it is showing

Every component sorted into one of four jobs, with the plain-language explanation first and the Litmus specifics after it.

The reason to draw it is that each plane fails differently. Lose the data plane and someone read one customer’s content. Lose the control plane and someone changed the rules for everybody and may have erased the proof. Lose the management plane and someone changed what is running, so neither of the other two was ever safe.

How to improve it

  • The finding in this view is that two components sit in two planes at once. FastAPI arranges work and also returns findings. One S3 bucket holds configs and reports, one prefix apart.
  • Naming those dual roles yourself is worth more than a reviewer finding them, because the mitigation is the same either way and the credibility is not.
Security build, what is missing and what it costsfour phases, roughly 950 to 2,700 a month

What it is showing

The architecture is well built for what it does and thin on the components that let you see, contain and prove. This is the sequenced list of what to add, with indicative monthly cost so the conversation is about ordering rather than about whether.

Every paid line carries a free or open-source alternative, because about two thirds of the total has a credible substitute at this stage.

How it works, step by step

  1. Phase 1 is detection and evidence: CloudTrail, flow logs, GuardDuty, Security Hub, Config and WAF. Nothing else works until you can see and evidence.
  2. Phase 2 is segmentation and containment: a subnet for the scan tier, separate accounts, egress filtering, a second NAT, the Bedrock endpoint, and Access Analyzer.
  3. Certificates run alongside: inventory and expiry alerting, DNS lockdown, transparency monitoring, TLS as code, mTLS on the callback, and image signing.
  4. Phase 3 is investigation and recovery: a SIEM, Macie on the report bucket, Inspector, Multi-AZ RDS and AWS Backup.

How to improve it

  • Phase 1 is the shortest path to passing a SOC 2 observation window and a customer security review, which makes it the phase to fund first regardless of appetite.
  • The Bedrock endpoint is the one line item that pays for itself, because it removes more NAT processing charge than it costs.
  • Private CA is the four hundred dollar decision. Treat it as customer-driven rather than as a default.
Subprocessors, who sees whateleven parties, eight in the data path

What it is showing

Every third party the diagrams touch and what each one actually sees. This is the list a customer’s privacy team asks for, and the list that has to appear in a data processing agreement before the first regulated customer signs.

Splitting it into those in the data path and those in the build and operate chain is what makes it readable, because the two groups raise completely different questions.

How to improve it

  • Auth0 and Stripe are outside the boundary on purpose, and that is a selling point rather than an admission: no password and no card number reaches the AWS account.
  • The missing piece is a sub-processor change notification commitment and a page a customer can subscribe to. Most enterprise agreements require notice, and there is no mechanism for it today.
Retention, how long to keep each thingthirteen categories

What it is showing

A suggested period for every store in the diagrams, with the obligation that sets the clock and the reasoning behind the number.

Retention is the control that turns a data map into a defensible position. A diagram says where data is; a schedule says when it stops being your problem.

How to improve it

  • Findings and report objects hold the same evidence in two stores, so they must expire on the same clock, and the S3 lifecycle rule is the control rather than the application deleting rows.
  • Access logs currently capture the progress-stream token in the query string. Until that is fixed, a long retention on access logs is a credential store with a twelve-month life.
  • These are engineering suggestions for counsel to confirm, not legal advice, and the section says so.
Attack classes, coverage and gapsfive in, five to add next

What it is showing

What the probe set covers today and where the gaps are, graded against the OWASP LLM Top 10, the OWASP Agentic Applications work and MITRE ATLAS.

It is tiered by what would change the product’s standing fastest rather than by difficulty, because the point of the view is sequencing.

How to improve it

  • The highest-value additions are the ones a buyer already has a name for, since a class you can name in their vocabulary is a class they can put in a requirement.
  • Coverage claims age quickly. Dating this view, and re-grading it each release, is what keeps it from becoming a liability in a questionnaire.
Models, attacker and judgeeight candidates, five rules

What it is showing

The adaptive loop is only as good as the pair of models driving it. The attacker decides what gets tried. The judge decides what counts as a finding, which makes it the measurement instrument for the entire platform.

Eight candidates for the two roles, and five rules that matter more than which model you pick.

How to improve it

  • A judge change is a measurement change. Version the judge, record which version produced each finding, and a customer can explain a change in their score without calling it a regression.
  • Today the pair is Llama 3.3 70B as attacker and Claude Haiku 4.5 as judge, on a cross-region inference profile. Stating the pair on the record is what makes the score reproducible.
Key

Glossary

Plain definitions for the terms used across the three views, grouped the way the diagrams are grouped. Written for a reader who has to sign off on this without being an AWS engineer.

Network and delivery10 terms
ALB, Application Load Balancer
Layer 7 load balancer. The only thing in the account that accepts inbound traffic from the internet. It ends TLS and forwards plain HTTP to the application.
ACM, AWS Certificate Manager
Issues and renews the TLS certificate the load balancer presents. Renewal is automatic, so there is no manual certificate rotation to forget.
NAT Gateway
Lets resources in a private subnet reach the internet without being reachable from it. Everything outbound is rewritten to come from one address.
Elastic IP
A fixed public address. Because all egress leaves through one, a customer can allowlist a single address for the scanner.
Internet Gateway
The VPC component that actually moves packets between the VPC and the internet. The NAT Gateway routes through it.
VPC endpoint
A private door onto an AWS service. Traffic to S3, ECR and SSM reaches them without touching the internet or the NAT, and without a per-gigabyte charge.
Public / private subnet
Public subnets have a route to the internet gateway. Private ones do not, which is why no scan task can be reached from outside.
Security group
A stateful allow-list on a resource. The ALB group accepts 443 from anywhere and only talks onward to the application group on port 8000.
CloudFront and Cloudflare
Two content delivery layers in front of the single-page app. They serve the static bundle; neither is in the path of an API call.
SNAT, source network address translation
Rewriting the sender address on the way out. It is why every probe appears to the customer to come from one address.
Compute and orchestration11 terms
ECS, Elastic Container Service
AWS container orchestrator. It decides what container runs where and keeps services at their desired count.
Fargate
Serverless compute for containers. There is no EC2 instance to patch or scale, and a task is billed only while it runs.
Task definition
The blueprint for a container: image, CPU and memory, environment variables and IAM role. checkmate-scan and da3lab-scan are two of them.
RunTask
The API call that launches one container from a task definition. Used here to start a scan, rather than keeping a scan worker warm.
Service versus task
A service keeps containers running continuously, like the API. A task runs once and exits, like a scan.
FastAPI
The Python web framework the API runs on, served by Uvicorn on port 8000. It handles every request a person or an API key makes: sign in, create a scan, read findings, fetch a report link.
Celery
A Python job queue. Work that outlives an HTTP request, such as watching a scan to completion, is handed to a Celery worker.
Celery Beat
The scheduler that fires recurring jobs, here dispatching due scan schedules once a minute.
Visibility timeout
How long the broker waits before assuming a job was lost and handing it to another worker. It must exceed the longest scan, hence 330 minutes.
task_acks_late and prefetch
Acknowledge a job after it finishes rather than when it is picked up, and hold only one at a time. Together they stop a crash losing work or a long job starving short ones.
SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
A database pattern that lets several workers claim rows without two of them claiming the same one. It is what stops a schedule firing twice.
Data and storage8 terms
RDS
Managed relational database. Here PostgreSQL, in a private subnet, reachable only from the application subnet.
ElastiCache Redis
Managed in-memory store. Used as the job broker, the short-lived result store and the browser session map.
S3 and the bucket policy
Object storage. The policy here refuses any request that is not over HTTPS, so an accidental plain HTTP read fails rather than succeeds quietly.
SSE-KMS
Server-side encryption where the key is managed in KMS rather than by S3 alone, so key use is auditable and revocable.
KMS, Key Management Service
Where the encryption keys live. S3, RDS, ElastiCache and every SecureString parameter sit behind it.
Pre-signed URL
A time-limited link that carries its own authorisation. Anyone holding it can read the object until it expires, with no login.
Share token
A no-authentication read link the platform issues for a report. Like a pre-signed URL, possession is permission.
PHI, protected health information
Health data about an identifiable person. Litmus does not seek it, but captured model responses can contain it if the target is a clinical assistant.
Data protection roles and terms17 terms
Controller
The party that decides why and how personal data is processed. Your customer is the controller for the data their scans touch, because they chose the target and the purpose.
Processor
A party that processes personal data on the controller's instructions and for no purpose of its own. Litmus is a processor to its customers.
Subprocessor
A processor engaged by another processor. Every third party in the register that touches customer data is a subprocessor of Litmus, and each one has to be disclosed to the customer and covered by contract.
Independent controller
A party that decides its own purposes for the same data rather than following instructions. Stripe is an independent controller for payment data, which is why its retention clock is longer than the platform's and correctly so.
Joint controllers
Two parties that jointly decide purpose and means, and are jointly answerable to the individual. Rare in a scanning product, but worth ruling out explicitly rather than assuming.
Data processing agreement
The contract that binds a processor: what it may do, which subprocessors it uses, how it handles deletion, breach notification and audit. This is the document the vendor register and the retention schedule feed into.
Subprocessor change notice
The commitment to tell customers before adding or swapping a subprocessor, and to let them object. It is the reason an unclassified party in the delivery chain is a contractual problem, not only a security one.
Covered entity
Under HIPAA, a health plan, clearinghouse or provider. A covered entity's obligations flow down to anyone handling protected health information on its behalf.
Business associate and BAA
A business associate handles protected health information for a covered entity, under a business associate agreement. If a hospital or device manufacturer runs scans whose evidence captures PHI, this is the contract that has to exist first.
Data subject
The identifiable person the data is about. In a red-teaming platform they are usually not the customer's user but whoever appears inside a captured model response, which is what makes the evidence store sensitive.
Personal data and PHI
Personal data is anything identifying a person. Protected health information is personal data tied to health, care or payment for care, and carries a stricter regime. The platform can acquire both without ever asking for either.
Data residency
The commitment about which countries or regions data is stored and processed in. Cross-region model inference is the most common way a single-region promise quietly becomes untrue.
Cross-border transfer and SCCs
Moving personal data outside its home jurisdiction, which needs a legal mechanism such as standard contractual clauses. Relevant here because model inference and edge delivery are both global by default.
Storage limitation
The principle that data is kept no longer than the purpose needs. It is why a retention schedule is a control rather than a housekeeping preference, and why the shortest defensible period beats the most convenient one.
Right to erasure
An individual's right to have their data deleted. The practical hard case is backups: deletion completes when the backup window rolls, which is why that window needs to be short enough to state out loud.
Record of processing activities
The inventory of what personal data is processed, why, on what basis, with whom it is shared and how long it is kept. The data overlay, the vendor register and the retention schedule are three views of it.
Data protection impact assessment
A structured assessment required when processing is likely to be high risk. Capturing verbatim model output that can contain health data is a strong candidate for one.
Identity and secrets11 terms
Auth0
The identity provider. It authenticates users and issues tokens, so no password ever reaches the platform.
JWT, JSON Web Token
A signed token carrying who the user is, which organisation they belong to and what they may do. It is presented on every API call.
RS256
Asymmetric signing. Auth0 holds the private key and the platform verifies with the public one, so a breach of the platform cannot forge tokens.
JWKS
The published set of public keys used to verify those signatures. The API fetches and caches it.
AuthContext
The object built after a token is verified, carrying the organisation, role and permissions. Every authorisation decision resolves through it.
Tenant isolation
Keeping one customer's data unreachable by another. Here it depends on the organisation identifier inside AuthContext being applied to every query.
Turnstile
Cloudflare's bot challenge, validated on the server at signup before any account is created.
Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store
Where credentials and configuration live. Values are injected into a container at start by its IAM role, so no human handles them and no image contains them.
IAM task role
The identity a container assumes. It grants exactly the AWS actions that container needs and nothing else.
OIDC and STS
How the build pipeline authenticates without stored keys: it presents a signed identity claim and receives short-lived credentials in exchange.
SigV4
AWS request signing. It proves who made an API call and that the request was not altered in flight.
Red teaming21 terms
Red teaming
Attacking your own system deliberately to find what an adversary would find first.
Probe
One crafted input sent to the target to test for a specific weakness.
Adapter
The translation layer between the probe runner and whatever shape the customer's endpoint takes: OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, plain HTTP, a browser, and others.
Prompt injection
Getting a model to follow instructions hidden in its input rather than the ones its operator intended.
Jailbreak
Getting a model to produce output its guardrails were meant to refuse.
Data exfiltration
Getting a model to reveal information it holds but should not disclose, such as its system prompt or another user's data.
Agent and tool abuse
Getting a model that can call tools to use them in ways its operator did not intend.
RAG injection
Poisoning the documents a retrieval system feeds a model, so the attack arrives through the knowledge base rather than the chat box.
PAIR
An adaptive attack loop. One model writes an attack, the target answers, a judge model scores the answer, and the score feeds back into the next attempt.
Attacker model
The model that writes the attacks. It is given the objective and the judge's feedback from the previous round, and returns a new attempt. Its job is creative pressure, not truth, so it is chosen for steerability and speed rather than accuracy. Here it is Llama 3.3 70B on Bedrock.
Judge model
The model that scores the target's answer against the original objective, one to ten with its reasoning. It is the measurement instrument: it decides what counts as a finding, so its calibration is the platform's calibration. Here it is Claude Haiku 4.5 on Bedrock, chosen for speed and cost because it runs on every exchange.
Why the two must differ
If the attacker and the judge come from the same model family they share training and therefore share blind spots, and the judge will quietly forgive exactly the attacks its sibling is best at. Separating the families is a measurement control, not a preference.
Configuration drift
The running system quietly ceasing to match the design it was deployed from, usually through a console change nobody wrote down. Every architecture diagram is a claim about one moment; drift is what makes it untrue.
Drift detection
Comparing what is actually running against the definition it should have come from, continuously rather than at audit time. Config rules, infrastructure drift detection and digest-pinned deployments are three different ways of asking the same question.
Judge drift
The same judge model scoring the same exchange differently after a version change. It looks like the customer's product got better or worse when only the instrument moved, which is why a fixed human-labelled gold set is worth keeping.
Amazon Bedrock
Managed access to foundation models. Used only by the deep scan loop, never by the basic scan.
Cross-region inference
Letting Bedrock serve a request from whichever region has capacity, which improves availability but widens where a prompt is processed.
Finding
One confirmed weakness, with severity, category, the evidence that demonstrates it and a mapping to a public framework.
Evidence
The verbatim prompt and the model's verbatim answer. It is what makes a finding credible, and also the most sensitive thing the platform stores.
OWASP LLM Top 10
The common reference list of language model application risks.
MITRE ATLAS
A catalogue of real adversary techniques against machine learning systems, structured like ATTandCK.
Delivery and reading the diagrams8 terms
OV-1 and OV-2
Architecture view conventions. OV-1 is the one-page operational picture for any reader. OV-2 traces the sequence of activities.
SV-1
The systems view: what is actually deployed, and where.
Trust boundary
A line where control changes hands. Data crossing one is where most real risk lives, which is why the diagrams mark them in amber.
Control plane versus data plane
The calls that arrange work versus the traffic that does it. Creating a scan is control plane; the probes hitting a customer endpoint are data plane.
SSE, server-sent events
A one-way stream from server to browser, used here for live scan progress. The browser API cannot set headers, which is why the token travels in the URL.
Webhook
An outbound HTTP call to a customer's own endpoint when something happens, so they do not have to poll.
Blue-green style deployment bake
Watching a new version for a fixed period after release and failing fast if it does not stabilise.
Well-Architected
AWS's six-pillar review framework: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability.
Roadmap

Attack classes worth adding

What the probe set covers today, and where the gaps are. Graded against the OWASP LLM Top 10, the OWASP Agentic Applications work and MITRE ATLAS, with an eye on where attacks are actually landing rather than where the taxonomies are tidiest. Tiered by what would change the product's standing fastest, not by difficulty.

Already in the probe set5 classes
Attack classStatusWhat it testsWhy it matters here
Direct prompt injectionin placeInstructions in the user turn that override the operator's intent.The baseline every buyer expects. Keep it, but it is no longer a differentiator.
Indirect and RAG injectionin placeInstructions carried in retrieved documents, tickets, emails or web pages rather than the chat box.This is where real incidents come from, because the attacker never touches the interface.
Data exfiltration and system prompt extractionin placeGetting the model to disclose its instructions, its context, or another user's data.Maps cleanly to a finding a customer can act on, and is the easiest to demonstrate to an executive.
Context override and refusal suppressionin placeRole-lock, persona pressure and instruction hierarchy attacks.Cheap to run and a good canary for guardrail regressions between model versions.
Adaptive jailbreak, single turnin placeThe PAIR loop: generate, score, refine until it lands or hits the cap.Your deep scan. Strong, but single-objective and largely single-turn.
Highest value to add next5 classes
Attack classStatusWhat it testsWhy it matters here
Multi-turn escalationto addHarm assembled across a conversation where no single turn is refusable.The dominant real-world jailbreak pattern and the one single-turn probes structurally cannot find. This is the biggest gap in the current tiering.
Memory and state poisoningto addPlanting instructions in persistent memory, a saved profile or session state that fire on a later, innocent turn.Every serious assistant product now ships memory. A poisoned memory is a persistent backdoor with no packet to catch.
Tool-call and parameter injectionto addInjecting into the arguments a model passes to a tool: SSRF through a fetch tool, path traversal through a file tool, query injection through a data tool.Your agent_abuse probes test whether a tool is misused. This tests what is smuggled inside a legitimate call, which is a different and more exploitable bug.
Insecure output handlingto addModel output rendered or executed downstream: markdown and HTML injection, generated SQL, generated shell, unescaped links.OWASP LLM02. The vulnerability is in the customer's application, not the model, which makes it a finding they can actually fix this sprint.
Excessive agency and autonomy boundariesto addIrreversible or costly actions taken without confirmation: sending, paying, deleting, escalating privilege.The question every board asks about agents. Currently untested, and it is the class most likely to produce a headline.
Worth adding for your market5 classes
Attack classStatusWhat it testsWhy it matters here
Clinical and regulated-domain harmto addAdvice outside the stated indication, dosage and contraindication errors, fabricated citations, PHI disclosure, unhedged diagnosis.Nobody serving medtech is testing this well. It is the probe set that would make Litmus the obvious choice for a device manufacturer rather than one of several generic scanners.
Guardrail and classifier evasionto addEncoding, ciphers, homoglyphs, low-resource languages, translation round-trips, token smuggling.Tests the filter rather than the model. Customers who bought a guardrail product need to know what it actually stops.
Multimodal injectionto addInstructions embedded in an image, a PDF or a screenshot the target ingests.You already bundle Playwright, so the browser adapter is most of the delivery mechanism. Document-borne injection is the practical vector for enterprise assistants.
Multi-agent and delegation abuseto addConfused-deputy across agent handoffs, orchestrator over-trust of a sub-agent, and instructions that survive a handoff.OWASP Agentic Applications territory, and the layer your own workbench already models. Litmus is well placed to be first here.
Context supply chainto addPoisoned retrieval corpus, hostile connector or MCP server, and malicious tool or skill descriptions that are read as instructions.A tool description is an untrusted input that most teams never classify as one.
Lower priority, but name them4 classes
Attack classStatusWhat it testsWhy it matters here
Denial of wallet and resource exhaustionpartialToken amplification, recursive tool loops, and unbounded context growth.Your resource_exhaustion detector sees the symptom. A dedicated probe class would let you quantify the cost.
Training data regurgitation and membership inferenceto addVerbatim recall of PII, secrets or licensed text, and whether a record was in the training set.Matters most to customers who fine-tuned on their own data, which is a growing slice of medtech.
Transfer and suffix attacksto addAdversarial suffixes optimised against open weights, replayed at a closed target.Cheap to generate offline and a useful hard-negative set for measuring whether a guardrail generalises.
Bias, toxicity and safety regression trackingpartialNot a jailbreak class. A stable, repeatable battery run on every scan to detect drift between model versions.This is what turns a one-off scan into a subscription: the customer needs to know their model got worse.
Roadmap

Attacker and judge models to consider

The adaptive loop is only as good as the pair of models driving it. The attacker determines what gets tried; the judge determines what counts as a finding, which makes it the measurement instrument for the whole platform.

Models to consider for each role8 candidates
ModelRoleAvailabilityWhyWatch out for
Llama 3.3 70B InstructAttackerBedrock, in use todayFast, cheap, steerable and open enough to be predictable across runs.It is also the most widely used attacker model, so your attack distribution looks like everyone else's.
A reasoning-class model for planning onlyAttackerBedrock or APIUse a stronger model to plan the multi-turn arc and a cheap model to write each turn. Planning is where multi-turn attacks are won.Costs more per objective. Cap it to the deep tier and to objectives that failed at the first pass.
A second, different-family attackerAttackerBedrock, Mistral or Qwen familyTwo families fail differently. Running both raises coverage more than doubling iterations on one.Doubles cost per objective. Sample it rather than running it every scan.
Deliberately weak and deliberately verbose variantsAttackeranyCheap diversity: a small model produces clumsier attacks that sometimes slip past filters tuned on fluent text.Noisy. Only worth it inside a scored loop that discards failures automatically.
Claude Haiku 4.5JudgeBedrock, in use todayFast, cheap, gives chain-of-thought reasoning with the score, which becomes the evidence in the finding.A single judge is a single point of measurement error. Its scores drift when the model version changes.
A stronger judge for disputed cases onlyJudgeBedrockEscalate only scores near the threshold, where a cheap judge is least reliable and the finding is most contestable.Adds latency on a minority of cases. Budget it as a percentage of judgements, not per scan.
A classifier-style safety model as a pre-filterJudgeLlama Guard family or Bedrock GuardrailsRuns in milliseconds and settles the obvious cases, so the expensive judge only sees genuine ambiguity.Trained on public taxonomies, so it will miss domain-specific harm such as clinical error entirely.
Deterministic detectors ahead of any modelJudgeyour own codeRegex, canary tokens and structural checks are free, reproducible and defensible in an audit.You already have this layer. The rule should be that no model judges what a detector can decide.
Rules that matter more than the model choice5 notes
  • Never use the same model family as attacker and judge. Shared training produces correlated blind spots, and the judge will systematically forgive the attacks its sibling is best at.
  • Hold a human-labelled gold set of a few hundred scored exchanges and re-run it whenever either model version changes. Without it you cannot tell a real security improvement in a customer's product from judge drift in yours.
  • Publish the judge threshold and its meaning in the report. A customer who cannot see why a seven is a finding and a six is not will not trust the number.
  • Record the attacker model, judge model and prompt version on every finding. Reproducibility is what separates a security report from a screenshot.
  • Cross-region inference means the attacker and judge may run in a different region from the rest of the platform. If you promise single-region processing, this is the promise that breaks first.
OV-1

Septa operational concept

Septa terminates the TLS session between an application and its model provider, inspects the prompt and the completion, and applies policy before either side sees the other. Seven numbered steps, three trust zones.

Septa OV-1 diagramthree trust zones, seven numbered steps
Call flow, step by stepthe same seven steps, read top to bottom

OV-1 shows the three trust zones and what sits in each. This shows the order. Every component gets a lane, time runs downward, and each numbered row is one hop. The numbers match OV-1.

Components in this viewwhat each box is, and which zone it sits in
Z0
Your applicationThe caller. Any application already using an OpenAI-compatible SDK. Integration is one line: base_url points at Septa instead of the provider.
Z0
Runtime DefenseThe operator’s view of posture, verdicts and audit history, and where policy is set without a deploy.
Z1
Control planeTenant records, API key resolution, routing rules and configuration. The authority the proxy consults on a cache miss.
Z1
Security ProxyThe interception point. Terminates the client session, resolves the tenant, inspects the prompt, applies the verdict, opens its own session to the provider, and inspects the completion on the way back.
Z1
Threat indexVector index of 105 prompt-attack patterns across 7 categories, baked into the container image so the decision needs no network call.
Z1
Audit ledgerThe hash-chained audit_events table that makes the trail tamper-evident, with a second independent copy in the S3 audit bucket.
Z2
Model providersOpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Bedrock and any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Outside the boundary in both directions.
Trust zoneswhat each zone is allowed to assume

ZONE 0 · UNTRUSTED

Hostile until the API key proves otherwise. TLS, API key, rate limiting.

ZONE 1 · TRUSTED

The only place that sees raw content. Private subnet, no inbound from the internet, allowlisted egress.

ZONE 2 · EXTERNAL

Step 3 is the only point content leaves AWS. Retention is contractual, per provider.

TLS

How the interception works

The one hop that decides everything else. Where the session is terminated is where the plaintext exists, and that is the fact every other view depends on.

How the interception workstwo TLS sessions, and where the plaintext exists

NOT A WIRETAP

The client addresses Septa voluntarily, so there is no certificate substitution and nothing to trust beyond Septa's own ACM certificate.

CREDENTIAL CUSTODY MOVES

Septa holds the provider key so the application never does. That removes a leak path and makes Zone 1 a credential store.

STREAMING IS THE HARD CASE

A completion cannot be judged before it has arrived. Buffering costs latency, incremental inspection can only truncate. State which one Septa does.

INTERCEPTION IS COOPERATIVE

Nothing stops an application pointing base_url back at the provider. "No prompt reaches a model unread" needs an egress block, not just the proxy.

The flow, hop by hopfourteen numbered arrows, start to end
1
Consumers to CloudFrontThe request leaves the customer over HTTPS to one public hostname, carrying the API key.
2
DNS to CloudFrontCloudflare resolves the Septa hostname to the distribution. A DNS answer, no traffic.
3
CloudFront to the ALBClient TLS terminates and a Lambda@Edge router forwards to a private VPC origin on port 80, in cleartext inside the VPC.
4
ALB to the ProxyLoad balanced to one Fargate task on :8080. The security group accepts the distribution alone.
5
Proxy to the APITenant identity and routing resolved on :8000 when the cache misses. No payload on this hop.
6
API to RDSAccount and configuration rows in the system of record.
7
Proxy to RedisA resolved identity, cached for 60 seconds. That TTL is also the revocation window.
8
Proxy to the providerThe prompt, leaving AWS. Only a call the proxy has allowed gets this far.
9
Proxy to JaegerSpan metadata, no payloads.
10
Proxy to S3The verdict and its metadata, one immutable object per proxied call.
11
Tasks to CloudWatchStructured logs and counters under the task role, for alarms on CPU and latency.
12
CloudWatch to SNSA threshold breach, fanned out to the ops channel.
13
EventBridge to SNSAn ECS lifecycle event, arriving on the same topic as the alarms.
14
Deploy through IAM and ECRA container image and a service update. GitHub Actions assumes the role through OIDC.
