Multi-tenant protection, as-is and to-be

Septa is a shared proxy on the request path of every tenant at once, which makes isolation both more important and harder to see. This sets out what holds today and what would make it structural.

What multi-tenancy means, in plain wordsthe idea itself, before the platform

Worth setting out on its own, because as-is and to-be only make sense once the question is clear.

1
What multi-tenancy actually meansOne copy of the software, one set of databases, many customers. It is the reason a SaaS product can charge a hundred pounds a month instead of ten thousand: everybody shares the same machines, and something has to keep their data apart. The alternative, one deployment per customer, is what enterprise software used to be, and it is why it cost what it cost.
2
Why it is a security question, not an architecture oneNothing physical separates two customers in a pooled system. What separates them is a decision made on every single request: this row belongs to that customer, so do not return it. Get it right ten thousand times and nobody notices. Get it wrong once and you have handed one customer another customer’s data, which is the one incident a SaaS company rarely survives intact.
3
The only question worth askingNot "are we multi-tenant", but "what happens the day someone forgets". If the answer is a leak, the boundary lives in code and depends on people being careful. If the answer is an empty result, an access denied, or a decryption failure, the boundary lives in the platform. Everything on this page is about moving from the first answer to the second.
4
As-is means what is true todayNot what the design intends, and not what the policy says. What the running system would actually do if a query shipped without a filter this afternoon. That is the version worth writing down, because it is the version a customer’s security team will find.
5
To-be means what would make it structuralOrdered by value for effort, not by ambition. Most of the list is configuration rather than rearchitecture, and the two or three items at the top change the failure mode rather than adding a feature.
What it means herethe same idea, applied to this platform
S
What this means for Septa specificallySepta is a shared proxy sitting on the request path of every tenant at the same moment. That is a stronger form of sharing than a shared database: two customers’ prompts are in the same process, in memory, simultaneously. The boundary is the API key resolving to a tenant, and everything downstream, routing, policy and audit, trusts that resolution.
S
And what makes it easier than the usual caseSepta stores no customer content. Prompts and completions are inspected in memory and never written to a Septa store, so the worst multi-tenancy outcome in most platforms, one customer reading another’s data at rest, has nothing to read. What is left to protect is metadata, credentials and availability, which is a genuinely smaller problem and worth saying out loud.
S
The two that a customer will ask aboutThe sixty second identity cache, which is also the window in which a revoked key still works. And the fact that one noisy tenant is a latency incident for every other tenant at once, because they share the proxy fleet. Both have straightforward answers on the to-be list, and neither has one today.
The isolation ladderfive levels, and what each one costs

Every multi-tenant decision is a choice of level on the same ladder. Naming the level you are on is more useful than arguing about whether you are isolated.

L0
Shared, separated by a value in application codeOne database, one bucket, one cache, one key. Every query carries a tenant identifier and the application is trusted to apply it. Cheapest to run and cheapest to get wrong: a single missing WHERE clause is a cross-tenant read, and nothing below the application would stop it. This is where both platforms sit today.
L1
Shared, separated by a value the platform enforcesSame infrastructure, but the separation moves out of application code and into something that fails closed. Row-level security in Postgres, an IAM condition on the S3 prefix, a client wrapper that refuses an unnamespaced Redis key. Almost no extra cost, and it converts the failure mode from silent leak to empty result. This is the level worth reaching for both platforms.
L2
Shared infrastructure, separate namespaces and keysOne instance, but a schema per tenant, a bucket prefix with its own key, a per-tenant KMS data key. Costs a key and some operational surface per tenant. Buys crypto-shredding for erasure and a clean story for a customer who asks about cryptographic separation, without running a fleet.
L3
Separate instances for the tenants who pay for themA dedicated database, bucket, cache or proxy service for one customer. Real money and real operational load per tenant, so it belongs in a premium tier rather than as a default. Worth designing for now so that the first customer who demands it is a configuration change rather than a rebuild.
L4
Separate AWS accountsThe only level where a mistake in one tenant cannot reach another by construction. Accounts are free; the cost is the pipeline, the logging and the operational discipline to run more than one. For most platforms the right first use of this level is separating staging from production, not separating customers.
Store by store, as-is and to-beeight stores, with the control that enforces each

Septa has an advantage here that most platforms do not: it stores no customer content, so the whole table is about metadata and credentials. The two rows worth doing first are the revocation channel and the per-tenant rate limit.

As-is todayTo-beWhat enforces it
RDS PostgreSQLTenants, configuration and the hash-chained audit_events table share one instance and one set of tables, separated by a tenant column applied in code.Row-level security on every tenant table, and a per-tenant chain in audit_events so truncation, retention and erasure are all per tenant rather than global.A Postgres policy plus a per-tenant chain head. It also makes the retention design tractable.
S3 audit bucketOne bucket of immutable log objects, one per proxied call, shared across tenants.A {tenant_id}/ prefix with an IAM condition, a lifecycle rule on the same clock as the database, and Object Lock in governance mode only where a customer contractually requires WORM.IAM prefix condition and a lifecycle rule. Object Lock is a per-customer decision because it removes your ability to honour erasure.
ElastiCache RedisOne cluster caching resolved tenant identity for 60 seconds, shared keyspace.Tenant-prefixed keys, and a revocation channel that clears a cached identity on key revocation rather than waiting out the TTL.A pub-sub invalidation, which closes the sixty second window a customer will ask about.
Secrets Manager and KMSProvider API keys and the platform envelope key held centrally for every tenant.A per-tenant secret path with an IAM condition on the path, a published rotation interval, and a customer-supplied key option where the customer keeps their own provider key and Septa never holds it.IAM path condition plus rotation. The customer-supplied option removes the concentration entirely for the customers who care.
Proxy computeOne Fargate service serving every tenant, one task role, one container image.Per-tenant rate limits and concurrency budgets at the proxy so one tenant cannot become a latency incident for the rest, and a dedicated service for a premium tier.A token bucket per tenant. This is an isolation control, not a billing one.
Network and accountOne account, one VPC. Staging and production resolve to the same load balancer.Separate accounts under Organizations for staging and production, and an egress allowlist restricted to the providers each tenant has actually approved.Accounts are free. A listener-rule mistake stops being possible rather than merely unlikely.
Logs and tracesShared CloudWatch groups and Jaeger traces. Payloads are absent by convention.A CI check that fails a build if a logging or tracing call can carry a request body, and a tenant tag on spans so support queries are scoped.A lint rule. It closes the largest PHI risk on the platform for almost nothing.
Threat indexOne FAISS index baked into the image, identical for every tenant.Per-tenant pattern overlays layered on the shared index, so a customer can add their own detections without a rebuild and without seeing anyone else’s.An overlay loaded at start-up from the tenant’s configuration.
As-iswhat protects one tenant from another today

Isolation is resolved per request from the API key, then carried by the application through routing, policy and audit.

1
One proxy fleet, every tenantThe same Fargate tasks serve all customers. Tenant identity is resolved per request from the API key, so isolation is a property of the request path rather than of the deployment.
2
The API key is the whole boundaryA customer API key resolves to a tenant in the Control API. Everything downstream, routing, policy and audit, keys off that resolution. There is no second factor on the data path.
3
A 60 second cache is also a revocation windowElastiCache holds resolved tenant identity for 60 seconds. That TTL is the period in which a revoked key still works, which makes it a security parameter rather than a performance one.
4
Audit rows are chained, not partitionedaudit_events is hash-chained and tamper-evident, with a second copy in S3. It is shared across tenants and separated by column, so the same forgotten-filter risk applies as anywhere else.
5
Provider keys are held centrallySepta holds the provider API keys so the customer application never does. That is a genuine gain for the customer and it makes this one account a concentrated credential store.
6
One account for staging and productionBoth resolve to the same load balancer today, so a listener-rule mistake is possible rather than structurally impossible.
To-besix changes, in the order I would make them

The revocation window and the per-tenant budget are the two that a customer will actually ask about.

1
Row-level security on tenant tablesSame argument as anywhere pooled: a missing filter should return nothing rather than someone else’s audit trail.
2
Make revocation beat the cachePublish a revocation event that clears the cached identity, or shorten the TTL for keys that have been revoked. Sixty seconds of valid access after revocation is the kind of number that appears in a questionnaire.
3
Per-tenant rate limits and quotas at the proxyToday the proxy is a shared resource on the request path. A noisy tenant is a latency incident for every other tenant at once, so a per-tenant budget is an isolation control, not just a billing one.
4
Separate accounts for staging and productionUnder Organizations, a routing mistake stops being possible. Accounts are free and it is the cleanest blast-radius story available.
5
Tenant isolation tests in CITwo tenants, one asserts it cannot see the other’s verdicts, audit rows or configuration, on every merge.
6
Enable the account-level recordCloudTrail, GuardDuty and Config are not on today. Without them there is no trustworthy answer to who changed a tenant’s configuration, which is a multi-tenancy question as much as a detection one.
Planes

Data, control and management planes

The same four jobs, applied to Septa. The classification is the one the SV-1 overlay uses, set out here with what each plane means and why the split matters for a platform whose whole purpose is to sit on the request path.

Planes diagramevery Septa component sorted into one of four planes
In plain words, with no jargonwhat a plane is, and why anyone bothered inventing the idea

Think of a restaurant. Everything that happens there falls into one of four jobs, and the same four jobs turn up in every piece of software once it is big enough to matter.

1
The food going to the table is the data planeA plate leaves the kitchen and arrives in front of a customer. That is the thing the customer came for, and it is the thing that can be dropped, poisoned or stolen. In software the plate is the customer’s actual data, and the data plane is every hand it passes through on the way.
2
The order book is the control planeSomebody takes the order, checks the customer is allowed to have it, tells the kitchen what to make, and writes down what was served. Nobody eats the order book. But if you change it, every plate after that is wrong, and if you tear pages out, nobody can prove what happened. That is the control plane: it decides and it records.
3
The builders and the cameras are the management planeSomeone built the kitchen, hired the cooks, and put up the cameras. They are not there at dinner service, but they decided what the kitchen can do and whether anyone would notice a problem. Change the kitchen and you have changed every meal, without ever touching a plate.
4
The farm is outside the boundaryThe vegetables come from a farm you do not own. You can choose the farm, read its certificate and stop buying from it, but you cannot walk into its fields and fix things. All you have is the contract.
?
Why anyone bothered making this distinctionBecause when something goes wrong, the first question is what was actually lost, and the answer is different for each plane. Lose the data plane and someone read one customer’s content. Lose the control plane and someone changed the rules for everybody, and may have erased the proof. Lose the management plane and someone changed what is running, so the other two were never safe to begin with. One incident, three completely different phone calls.
What the four planes meanthe question each one answers, and what a compromise of it costs

A plane is a job, not a place. All four usually run in the same account, often on the same subnet, so the split is only visible if the drawing says so. The reason to draw it is that each plane fails differently.

DP
Data plane, on the request pathThe path a customer request actually travels, and the only place customer content exists in the clear. It answers: what touches the content. A compromise here exposes the content itself, one request at a time or in bulk, and it is the plane a customer means when they ask who can read their prompts.
CP
Control plane, decides and recordsAuthenticates the caller, resolves the tenant, decides what is allowed, and writes the record of what happened. It answers: who decided, and on what basis. A compromise here does not read content directly. It does something worse: it changes what the data plane is willing to do, and it can rewrite or suppress the evidence that it did.
MP
Management plane, builds and watchesPipelines, images, roles, logs, detection and human access. It answers: what is running, who put it there, and who would notice. A compromise here is the supply chain answer: change the artifact and you own both other planes, or blind the detection and own them quietly.
OB
Outside the boundary, governed by contractThird parties that hold or receive something you care about. It answers: what is not yours to control. The control is a contract and a review, not a security group, and the honest position on a diagram is to draw them outside and say so.
The same four jobs, in Septawhat the plate, the order book and the cameras actually are here
1
The plate is every prompt and every answerAn application sends a prompt to its AI provider, and Septa sits in the middle and reads it. That prompt, and the answer that comes back, is the plate. Unusually, Septa is not beside the path, it is the path: the Security Proxy is the only place either one exists in readable form.
2
The order book is who the customer is, and what was blockedThe Control API knows which customer an API key belongs to, what rules apply to them, and where their traffic should go. The database keeps a chained record of every call, allowed and blocked, so nobody can quietly remove a line. None of it ever holds the prompt itself.
3
The builders are here, the cameras are notGitHub Actions builds and ships the proxy image, and there is a dashboard showing latency and errors. What is missing is the account-level recording: CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Config are not enabled, so a change to the account leaves no trustworthy trace of who made it.
4
The farm is the model providerOpenAI, Anthropic, Google or Bedrock receive the prompt once Septa has decided to allow it. What they keep, and for how long, is written in their contract rather than enforced by Septa. That is the one part of the picture Septa can choose but cannot control.
Protecting each plane, as-is and to-befour planes, and what changes

The plane split is only useful if it changes what you do. This is what protecting each one looks like today and what it would look like next.

PlaneAs-is todayTo-beWhat it buys you
Data planeThe proxy is both the request path and the enforcement point. Shared fleet, one task role, plaintext in memory only, single NAT egress.Per-tenant rate limits, an egress allowlist per tenant, a dedicated proxy service in a premium tier, and mTLS on the internal hop so content stops being readable between CloudFront and the ALB.A compromise of the proxy remains the worst case, but its blast radius and its egress both narrow.
Control planeControl API, RDS, ElastiCache, the audit bucket and Secrets Manager. Tenant identity resolved from an API key and applied in code.Row-level security, per-tenant audit chains, a revocation channel that beats the cache, and per-tenant secret paths.The control plane keeps its useful property, that it never sees content, and gains a boundary that fails closed.
Management planeGitHub Actions with OIDC, ECR, and the observability trio. CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Config are not enabled.Enable the three, sign images and verify at deploy, and split staging from production into separate accounts.Changes to the account become attributable, which is a multi-tenancy control as much as a detection one.
Outside the boundaryModel providers receive content once a call is allowed. Retention is per provider.A published provider retention table, a customer-selectable allowlist of providers, and a DPA naming each one.The customer chooses their own exposure instead of inheriting yours.
What this means for Septathe proxy is the data plane and the enforcement point at once
1
The Security Proxy is the data plane, and the control on itEvery prompt and every completion passes through it, and it is the only place plaintext content exists. It is also where the verdict is applied. That is unusual: for most platforms the enforcement point sits beside the data path, and here it is the data path. It makes the control effective and it makes the component the single most sensitive one in the account.
2
The control plane never sees contentControl API, RDS, ElastiCache and the audit bucket hold tenants, configuration, verdicts and evidence of decisions, not payloads. That separation is real and it is worth keeping: it means an operator or a support engineer can answer what happened without reading what was said.
3
Cached identity is a control plane decision with a shelf lifeElastiCache holds resolved tenant identity for 60 seconds. That TTL is the window in which a revoked key still resolves, so it is a control plane property that has a direct data plane consequence.
4
Most of the management plane is proposed, not deployedGitHub Actions, the deploy role, ECR and the observability trio are real. CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config and Security Hub are not enabled today, so the account can be changed without a tamper-evident record of who changed it. That is the gap the security overlay names.
5
The providers are the only thing outsideStep 3 is the single point at which content leaves AWS. What happens to it there is contractual, differs per provider, and is the one part of the picture Septa cannot enforce.
Schedule

Retention, and where regulated data could rest

A suggested retention schedule for every Septa store: what it holds, how long to keep it and which obligation sets the clock. The unusual thing about Septa is how short the list of content stores is. Prompt and completion content is inspected in memory and never written down, so almost everything below is metadata about a decision rather than the decision’s content. These are engineering suggestions to take to counsel, not legal advice, and the periods need confirming against your own contracts.

Suggested retention schedule13 categories
DataWhereSuggested periodDriverWhy that number
Prompt and completion contentSecurity Proxy memory onlyNot persisted. It exists for the duration of the call and is gone when the task returns the response.Least privilege; customer DPAThis is the strongest fact Septa has and it belongs in the DPA in one sentence: content is inspected in memory and never written to a Septa store. Everything else on this table is metadata about that content, not the content itself.
Verdicts and decision metadataRDS audit_events12 months by default, customer-selectable at 90 or 365 daysSOC 2 CC7.2; customer DPATwelve months covers a full SOC 2 observation window and lets a customer show a trend. Because the table is hash-chained, expiry has to be a documented truncation that re-anchors the chain, not a row delete, or the tamper-evidence claim breaks the day you first enforce retention.
Audit objects, one per proxied callS3 audit bucketSame clock as audit_events, enforced by an S3 lifecycle ruleSOC 2 CC7.2; GDPR Art. 5(1)(e)Two copies of the same evidence must expire together. The lifecycle rule is the control; the application deleting rows is not. Add Object Lock in governance mode only where a customer contractually needs WORM, because it also removes your ability to honour an erasure request.
Resolved tenant identityElastiCache Redis60 seconds, already enforced by TTLNoneNo change needed, and worth stating explicitly because customers ask what the cache holds. The same 60 seconds is the window in which a revoked API key still resolves, so it appears on the multi-tenancy list as well as this one.
Tenant records, routing rules and configurationRDSLife of the account, plus 30 days after terminationContract; SOC 2 CC6.5Thirty days is the usual grace period for a customer who changes their mind. What is missing today is the runbook: deletion on termination should be a documented, evidenced procedure rather than a manual query.
Customer API keysRDS, stored hashedDeleted on revocation. The fact of the revocation stays in the audit trailSOC 2 CC6.1The key itself is never recoverable, only a hash, so a database compromise does not yield a usable credential. Keep the revocation event, because who revoked what and when is exactly what an incident review asks for.
Provider API keysSecrets Manager, KMS envelopeLife of the tenant relationship, rotated on a defined scheduleLeast privilege; SOC 2 CC6.1Septa holds these so the customer application never does, which is a real gain and a concentration of risk. A rotation schedule is what turns storage into custody, and it is worth publishing the interval.
Application and task logsCloudWatch Logs90 days hot, then export to S3 for 12 monthsSOC 2 audit period; ISO 27001 A.8.15Twelve months covers the observation window. The condition attached to this row is the important one: prompt and completion bodies must never be written here. If they are, this becomes a content store with a twelve-month clock, and the whole in-memory-only claim above collapses.
Distributed tracesJaeger7 to 14 daysNoneSpan metadata only, no payloads. That is the design, and it is worth an automated check rather than an assertion, because a well-meant debug attribute is the usual way payloads end up in traces.
Metrics and dashboardsPrometheus and Grafana15 days at full resolution, 90 days downsampledNoneCounters and latencies only. An inline proxy sits on the critical path, so its own latency history is operationally useful well beyond the incident that prompted the look.
Edge and load balancer access logsS390 days, then 12 months in cheaper storageSOC 2; incident responseAccess logs answer what a scan task or a caller actually connected to. Keep them long enough to investigate an incident found late, which in practice is longer than most teams first choose.
Container imagesECREvery digest currently or recently deployed, plus the last 20 buildsSupply chain; SOC 2 CC8.1You need the exact digest that was running when something went wrong. A tag is not enough, because tags move. Lifecycle everything older than that.
Prompt content held by the model providerOutside the boundaryContractual, and it differs per providerCustomer DPA; provider termsThis is the one row Septa cannot enforce. It can choose the provider, read the terms, turn training off where that is an option, and tell the customer what the answer is. It cannot make the provider forget. Bedrock is the one to watch, because model invocation logging is off by configuration rather than by design.
Where PHI could land, and where it cannotfour places, and only one of them is by design

Septa is not a health system, but a customer can point it at a clinical assistant, and from that moment every prompt and every completion on that route is potentially regulated data. The useful question is not whether Septa handles PHI. It is which stores could still hold it an hour later.

1
The proxy, for the length of one callThe only place content exists in readable form, and it exists there for milliseconds. Nothing is written. This is by design and it is the reason the rest of this list is short.
2
CloudWatch, if anyone ever logs a payloadThe realistic failure mode. One debug line, one exception handler that logs the request body, and a transient system becomes a twelve-month store of regulated content. A log scrubber plus a test that asserts payload fields never appear is the control worth building first.
3
Traces, for the same reasonJaeger carries span metadata by design. A single added attribute carrying the prompt would change that quietly and nothing would flag it.
4
The model provider, contractuallyOnce step 3 completes, the content is at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or Bedrock. What they keep is their terms, not Septa’s control. Telling a customer exactly which provider held their content, and pointing at that provider’s retention, is the honest answer.
✗
Not in RDS, not in S3, not in the cacheThe audit trail holds verdicts and metadata about the decision, not the content of the decision. That is unusual for a security product and it is worth stating plainly, because most reviewers will assume the opposite.
What is not set todaythe gap between this schedule and the account

Everything above is a proposal. This is the honest statement of what the dev account actually enforces right now.

1
No lifecycle rules on the audit bucketObjects accumulate. Nothing expires. The first customer with a storage limitation clause will ask for the rule, not the policy document.
2
No enforced clock on audit_eventsRows are kept indefinitely. Because the table is hash-chained, adding retention later is a design task rather than a cron job, so it is worth deciding the truncation approach before the table gets large.
3
No documented deletion runbookTermination, and a customer erasure request, both need a procedure that names every store on this table and produces evidence it ran. That document does not exist yet, and it is usually requested before the first enterprise contract is signed.
4
Log scrubbing is a convention, not a controlPayloads are not logged today because nobody logs them. Nothing enforces it. A CI check on the logging calls is cheap and closes the largest PHI risk on the list.
5
No sub-processor retention statementEach provider has its own retention behaviour, and the customer is entitled to know which one held their content. A short table of provider retention, kept current, saves answering it per deal.
Deletion, and what an erasure request actually means herethe hash chain makes this a design question
1
Content is the easy halfSepta stores no prompt or completion, so an erasure request touches nothing in RDS, S3 or the cache. That is a genuinely strong position and it should be the first line of the answer.
2
Metadata is the harder halfVerdicts, timestamps, tenant identifiers and route information are personal data in some readings, and they are in a chained table. Deleting a row breaks the chain, so the options are truncation with a re-anchor, or crypto-shredding a per-tenant key.
3
Crypto-shredding is the cleaner answerEncrypt tenant-scoped audit fields under a per-tenant key, and erasure becomes deleting one key rather than rewriting a chain. It costs a KMS key per tenant, so it is a decision to take deliberately rather than a default.
4
The provider is out of scope of your deleteWhatever the provider retained is theirs to delete. The customer’s request has to be forwarded, and the DPA should say so rather than implying Septa can delete it.
Sub

Controllers, processors and sub-processors

Who holds what, and in what role. The customer is the controller in every case: Septa processes prompts and completions only to apply the policy that customer set. Everything below Septa is a sub-processor, and the model providers are the only ones that receive content and are governed by contract rather than by control.

PartyWhat it does for SeptaWhy it is on this listWhere
AWS Sub-processorECS Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache, S3, Secrets Manager, KMS, SSM, CloudWatch, ECR, CloudFront, ACM, NAT and VPC networkingHosts the entire platform. Prompt and completion content passes through CloudFront and the proxy tasks, and audit records rest in RDS and S3.us-east-1
Cloudflare Sub-processorAuthoritative DNS for the prompthalo.dev zoneName resolution only. It carries no request traffic and sees no prompt or completion content.Global anycast
OpenAI Sub-processorModel inference for calls routed to OpenAIReceives prompt content once a call is allowed. Retention and training behaviour are contractual, set by the customer’s own agreement or by Septa’s.Per provider terms
Anthropic Sub-processorModel inference for calls routed to AnthropicSame position as OpenAI. Receives prompt content on allowed calls only.Per provider terms
Google Sub-processorModel inference for calls routed to GoogleSame position. Receives prompt content on allowed calls only.Per provider terms
Amazon Bedrock Sub-processorModel inference for calls routed to BedrockInside AWS but a separate service boundary. Model invocation logging must stay off, or it becomes a content store.us-east-1
GitHub Sub-processorSource hosting and the Actions pipeline that builds and deploys the proxyHandles no customer content. It is a supply-chain path into the trusted zone, which is why it uses OIDC rather than stored AWS keys.Global
PromptHalo ProcessorOperates Septa on the customer’s instructionProcesses prompts and completions solely to apply the policy the customer configured, and to produce the audit record.us-east-1
The customer ControllerDecides what is sent, which provider is used and what policy appliesDetermines the purpose and means of processing. Septa acts only on that instruction.Customer defined
What a customer will ask about this listthree questions, and the honest answers
1
Does Septa train on my promptsNo. Septa inspects a prompt to apply a verdict and writes a record of the decision, not the content of the decision. What the model provider does with the prompt after step 3 is a separate question, answered by that provider’s contract.
2
Which sub-processors see my contentAWS, because it hosts the proxy, and whichever model provider the call was routed to. Cloudflare and GitHub see none. That is a short and defensible list, and it is worth publishing rather than being asked for it.
3
What is not on this list yetA sub-processor change notification commitment, and a published page a customer can subscribe to. Most enterprise agreements require notice before a new sub-processor is added, and the mechanism for that does not exist today.

What these views are showing

A written walkthrough of each Septa view: what it is for, how it works step by step, and what I would change. Download it as Word or PDF if you want to circulate it without the diagrams.

every section below, in one document
OV-1, the operational conceptwhat Septa does to one call

What it is showing

OV-1 answers what Septa is for. An application already talks to a model provider. Septa is put in the middle of that conversation, reads both halves, and applies a policy before either side sees the other.

Three zones, because the interesting fact is where the content is readable. It is readable in exactly one of them.

How it works, step by step

  1. The application makes its normal call, addressed to Septa instead of the provider. The only change is base_url.
  2. The prompt is checked against the threat index before anything leaves the account.
  3. Only an unblocked prompt crosses into Zone 2, to whichever model was asked for.
  4. The answer returns to the proxy, never straight to the application.
  5. The completion is inspected in turn, then handed back if it passes.
  6. A hash-chained entry is written for every call, allowed and blocked alike.
  7. The operator sets policy, which the control plane pushes to the proxy.

How to improve it

  • The single most useful addition would be a latency budget on the diagram. An inline proxy is on the critical path of every call, so its own p99 is a customer-facing number and belongs beside the flow.
  • Step 6 is drawn as a soft path because it is asynchronous. Saying explicitly that a failed audit write does not fail the call, or does, is a question a buyer will ask.
  • A blocked-call path would make the drawing complete. Today the diagram shows the allowed case, and the block case is the product.
TLS interception, the hop that decides everythingwhy this is not a man in the middle

What it is showing

One hop, drawn on its own because everything else depends on it. There are two separate TLS sessions, not one relayed session: the application to Septa, and Septa to the provider.

That is what makes the plaintext exist, and it is also what makes the interception legitimate: the client addressed Septa deliberately and validated Septa’s own certificate. Nothing was substituted.

How it works, step by step

  1. The application opens session A. It is the client, Septa is the server.
  2. Septa presents its ACM certificate for its own hostname. The SDK validates it normally.
  3. Septa decrypts, inspects the prompt, and applies the verdict.
  4. Septa opens session B to the provider as a client, using a provider key held in Secrets Manager.
  5. The completion returns on session B, is inspected, and is re-encrypted onto session A.

How to improve it

  • SEPTA-91 is the open item: ACM Private CA is disabled, so the CloudFront to ALB hop runs in cleartext inside the VPC. Closing it removes the second place content is readable.
  • The provider keys sit with Septa rather than with the customer. That is a real gain for the customer and a concentration of risk for Septa, and it deserves a rotation story rather than only a storage story.
  • A customer-supplied key option, where the customer keeps the provider key and Septa never holds it, is the version of this that removes the concentration entirely.
OV-2, the request paththe numbered flow, against real components

What it is showing

OV-2 puts the five numbered steps against the components that serve them, and adds the four paths that run beside the request rather than on it.

The distinction matters: the numbered path carries content, the four side paths carry configuration and evidence.

How it works, step by step

  1. The application calls Septa. Only base_url changed.
  2. The proxy searches the FAISS index in process, so the decision needs no network call and cannot fail open on a timeout.
  3. An unblocked prompt goes to the provider.
  4. The completion returns to the proxy.
  5. The inspected response goes back to the application.
  6. Beside all of that: the dashboard reads from the Control API, the Control API queries RDS, the proxy writes a hash-chained audit row asynchronously, and the proxy caches tenant identity in ElastiCache.

How to improve it

  • The 60 second cache TTL is the revocation window. Making revocation push rather than wait is the change that turns a known gap into a non-issue.
  • The audit write is asynchronous and therefore can be lost. A queue with a durable buffer, or an explicit statement that it is best-effort, is better than leaving it ambiguous.
  • Nothing on this view shows what happens when the provider is slow or down. A timeout and fallback path is the missing sixth step.
SV-1, the system viewthe same platform as deployed

What it is showing

The deployment view, with eight overlays over one drawing: data flow, planes, components, encryption, protocol, security, privacy and Well-Architected.

Every component carries a classification on each overlay, so the same picture answers eight different reviewer questions.

How it works, step by step

  1. A request resolves through Cloudflare DNS to CloudFront.
  2. CloudFront terminates client TLS and a Lambda@Edge router forwards to a private VPC origin.
  3. The internal ALB spreads requests across the Fargate tasks. Its security group accepts the distribution alone.
  4. The Security Proxy resolves the tenant, consulting ElastiCache and falling back to the Control API.
  5. FAISS is searched in process, and the verdict is applied.
  6. Allowed calls leave through the single NAT gateway to the provider.
  7. Audit rows go to RDS and objects to S3. Credentials come from Secrets Manager under the task role.
  8. GitHub Actions builds images to ECR and updates the service, assuming a role through OIDC.

How to improve it

  • Four detective controls are drawn as proposed rather than deployed: CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config and Security Hub. That is the largest single gap in the view.
  • VPC endpoints are not deployed, so S3, Secrets Manager and ECR traffic traverses the NAT alongside customer content. Adding them shrinks the egress allowlist to providers only.
  • Single-AZ and a single NAT are the availability exposure, and the bastion is the one human path into the private subnet, which makes its session logging worth verifying rather than assuming.
Call flow, the panel under OV-1the same steps, as a timeline

What it is showing

OV-1 shows the three trust zones and what sits in each. The call flow panel underneath shows the order. Every component gets a lane, time runs downward, and each numbered row is one hop.

The numbers match OV-1 exactly, so the two read together without translation.

How it works, step by step

  1. The application sends a prompt to the Security Proxy.
  2. The proxy inspects it against the threat index.
  3. An unblocked prompt is forwarded to the provider.
  4. The completion returns to the proxy.
  5. The inspected response goes back to the application.
  6. A hash-chained record is written to the audit ledger.
  7. The control plane pushes policy to the proxy, driven by the operator.

How to improve it

  • A blocked path is the missing row. Every row here is the allowed case, and blocking is the product.
  • Rough latency per hop would make this the view an engineer uses when the proxy is slow, rather than only the view a reviewer reads once.
Overlay: Data and PHI39 marks, 29 components and 10 hops

What it is showing

Every place data sits and every hop it moves along, numbered D1 to D39 and coloured by sensitivity: pink where content is readable and PHI or PII is possible, sand for pseudonymous metadata, mint for no customer data, lilac for outside the boundary.

The point of the view is the shape of the exposure. Content is readable in three components and crosses the boundary once. Everything else holds metadata about a decision.

How to read it

  1. Start at D2, the application authoring the prompt, and follow the numbers along the request path.
  2. The pink boxes are the only components that ever see readable content: CloudFront, the internal ALB and the Security Proxy.
  3. D31 is the one to look at twice. The hop from CloudFront to the ALB runs in cleartext inside the VPC.
  4. D38 is the only hop on which content leaves AWS.

How to improve it

  • Close SEPTA-91 and the number of places content is readable drops from three to two.
  • The 60 second identity cache at D36 is also the revocation window. Make revocation push rather than wait and that line stops being a caveat.
  • D23 is the risk nobody plans: CloudWatch is pseudonymous today only because nobody logs a payload. A CI check on the logging calls makes it structural.
Overlay: Encryptionat rest and in transit, per component

What it is showing

Where content is protected and where it is not, split into the three answers that matter: encrypted in transit with nothing at rest, encrypted at rest with KMS, or plaintext living in that component.

The red boxes are the honest part of the view. Encryption everywhere is not the claim; encryption everywhere except the two places inspection requires plaintext is the claim.

How to improve it

  • ACM Private CA is disabled, which is why one internal hop is plaintext rather than mTLS. That is the single highest-value change on this layer.
  • Per-tenant keys are not in place. They cost a KMS key per tenant and only matter to customers who ask for cryptographic separation, so decide it deliberately rather than by default.
Overlay: Protocolsport and protocol on every component and hop

What it is showing

The literal wire answer: HTTPS 443 at the edge, HTTP 80 from CloudFront to the ALB, HTTP 8080 into the proxy, 5432 to Postgres, 6379 to Redis, and an in-process call to the threat index.

This is the layer a network reviewer asks for and the one that makes the cleartext hop impossible to miss.

How to improve it

  • The in-process FAISS call is worth stating plainly in a questionnaire. A detection path with no network dependency cannot fail open on a timeout.
  • Port 80 inside the VPC is defensible and common, but it should be stated rather than discovered.
Overlay: Securitywhat control applies where

What it is showing

Each component classified by the control that actually protects it: authentication on an exposed surface, network and policy control, identity and role control, key and secret custody, or no control today.

The red boxes are the ones with no control today. There are two of them and they are both detective rather than preventive.

How to improve it

  • The proxy is the enforcement point and the data path at the same time, which makes its own hardening the highest-leverage work on the platform.
  • Per-tenant rate limits belong on this layer. Today a noisy tenant is a latency incident for every other tenant at once.
Overlay: Keys and certificateswhich key protects each store, and who holds it

What it is showing

Where key material lives and which components hold none at all. Secrets Manager and KMS are the custodian: everything else either reads from it or holds nothing.

Septa holds the provider API keys so the customer application never does. That is a real gain for the customer and a concentration of risk for Septa, and this is the view where that trade is visible.

How to improve it

  • A published rotation interval turns storage into custody. Right now the answer is where keys live, not how often they change.
  • A customer-supplied key option, where the customer keeps their provider key and Septa never holds it, removes the concentration entirely for the customers who care.
  • Image signing is not in use, so there is a gap between what the pipeline built and what runs.
Overlay: Well-Architectedwhat exists, and what is missing

What it is showing

Every component labelled with the pillar concern it is deciding, and then the part that makes this layer different from the others: the components that are not there yet.

Six new components are drawn in fluorescent green with NEW badges and glowing arrows to what they attach to, and the four already marked proposed on the diagram are ringed in the same colour. Together they are the gap between the architecture as built and the architecture as it should be.

How to improve it

  • Multi-AZ RDS and a second NAT in AZ B are the availability pair. Single-AZ and a single NAT are the exposure a zone failure would find.
  • AWS Backup with an immutable vault in a second account is the recovery half. Backups beside the thing they protect share its blast radius.
  • Macie on the audit bucket answers whether PHI is actually present rather than assuming, and Inspector answers what is in the images that are running.
  • mTLS on the internal hop closes SEPTA-91 and removes the second place content is readable.
  • CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Config are the detective floor. Without them the account can be changed with no trustworthy record of who changed it.
Multi-tenant protection, as-is and to-besix mechanisms, six changes

What it is showing

Septa is a shared proxy on the request path of every tenant at once, which makes isolation both more important and harder to see than in a platform where tenants only share storage.

As-is sets out the six mechanisms that carry the guarantee today. The API key resolving to a tenant is the root of all six.

How to improve it

  • The sixty second identity cache is also the revocation window. Making revocation push rather than wait is the change a customer will actually ask about.
  • Per-tenant rate limits are an isolation control here, not a billing one, because a noisy tenant is a latency incident for every other tenant simultaneously.
  • Separate accounts for staging and production make a routing mistake structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely, and accounts are free.
Planes, data, control and managementwhy the proxy is unusual

What it is showing

The four jobs, explained plainly first and then applied to Septa.

The finding is that the Security Proxy is the data plane and the enforcement point at the same time. For most platforms the control sits beside the data path. Here it is the data path, which makes the control effective and makes that one component the most sensitive thing in the account.

How to improve it

  • The control plane genuinely never sees content, which means an operator can answer what happened without reading what was said. That is a strong statement and it should be made explicitly.
  • Most of the management plane is proposed rather than deployed, so the account can be changed today without a tamper-evident record of who changed it.
Retention, and where regulated data could restthirteen categories

What it is showing

A suggested period for every Septa store. The unusual feature is how short the content list is: prompt and completion content is inspected in memory and never written down, so almost everything on the table is metadata about a decision rather than its content.

That single fact is the strongest thing Septa has to say to a privacy reviewer, and it belongs in the DPA in one sentence.

How to improve it

  • audit_events is hash-chained, so expiry has to be a documented truncation that re-anchors the chain. Deciding that before the table gets large is much cheaper than after.
  • The realistic PHI risk is not the design, it is a log line. One exception handler that logs a request body turns a transient system into a twelve-month content store. A CI check on logging calls is the cheapest control on the list.
  • Nothing above is enforced today. No lifecycle rules, no clock on the audit table, no deletion runbook. The section says so rather than implying otherwise.
Controllers, processors and sub-processorsnine parties, two see content

What it is showing

Who holds what and in what role. The customer is the controller in every case, Septa is the processor, and everything beneath is a sub-processor.

Only two sub-processors ever see content: AWS, because it hosts the proxy, and whichever model provider the call was routed to. Cloudflare and GitHub see none.

How to improve it

  • That short list is defensible and worth publishing rather than waiting to be asked for it.
  • The gap is the same as on the Litmus side: no sub-processor change notification commitment and no subscribable page, which most enterprise agreements require.
Component referenceevery box, and why it is there

What it is showing

A row per component with what it is and why it exists in the architecture, grouped by zone.

It is the companion to SV-1: the diagram answers where, and this answers why. Together they are what a reviewer needs to stop asking about individual boxes.

How to improve it

  • Four components are listed as proposed rather than deployed: CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config with Security Hub, and VPC endpoints. Keeping that status visible in the table, rather than only on the diagram, is what stops the two drifting.
  • ACM Private CA is drawn greyed for the same reason. Its absence is why one internal hop runs in cleartext, and the table says so.

Every component in the system view, with what it is, what it holds and how it is reached.

Terminates the client's TLS session, resolves the tenant, inspects the prompt, applies the verdict, opens its own session to the provider, inspects the completion, and emits the audit record.It is the whole product. Litmus threat model and attack graph

What is reachable from outside, what a foothold looks like, how it escalates, and what it costs. Built from the architecture in this document rather than from a scan, so every node here is a component or a control you can point at.

Attack paths, scoredsix paths, each read left to right, with five scores
View
External exposurewhat is reachable, and what it tells an attacker

The starting column of the graph, in words. Everything here is discoverable without touching the platform: DNS records, certificate transparency, a sign-in page, a support ticket.

What it isWhy it matters
Web applicationCloudFront distribution and Amplify hosting, plus the Auth0 tenantDiscoverable from DNS and certificate transparency. The sign-in page tells an attacker which identity provider to target.
Scan APIthe orchestrator endpoint the browser calls with an Auth0 JWTReachable with any valid token. Authorisation is the org_id claim applied in application code on every query.
Report deliverypre-signed S3 URLs and no-auth share tokensBearer capabilities over the most sensitive artefact the platform holds. A forwarded link is a valid credential.
Third-party accountsAuth0, Stripe, GitHub, the AWS consoleOutside the AWS boundary and outside CloudTrail. Each has its own MFA and session policy to get right.
Scan egressFargate tasks leaving through one NAT gatewayThe source address customers will see, and the one they will allowlist. Its reputation is shared by every tenant.
Attack paths in table formthe same six paths, for a questionnaire

Ratings are judgement, not arithmetic. Likelihood is how often this class of thing happens to platforms built this way; impact is what it costs if it does. Nothing here needs a zero day.

PathChainLikelihoodImpactWhat happensWhat breaks it
P1Stolen token to cross-tenant evidence1 to 5 to 10 to 13HighSevereA token or session is stolen, then any query that omits the org_id predicate returns another tenant’s findings.Row-level security in Postgres. It turns a forgotten filter from a leak into an empty result set.
P2Share link replay3 to 7 to 13HighSevereA report link is forwarded, indexed, or captured in an access log that records the query string.Short TTL, one-time tokens bound to a recipient, object-level logging, and keeping tokens out of the query string.
P3Pipeline to scan task4 to 8 to 9 to 14MediumSevereA poisoned dependency or a triggerable workflow ships code into a task whose role can RunTask and send mail.Pinned and reviewed dependencies, image signing verified at deploy, and a scoped per-scan role.
P4Scan tier to data tier8 or 9 to 11 to 13MediumSevereScan containers run attacker payloads in the same subnet as the API and the workers.A dedicated subnet and security group for the scan tier with no route to the data tier, plus egress filtering.
P5Target credential reuse9 to 12 to 15MediumHighScan configs hold the customer endpoint credential until the scan deletes them.A separate bucket with a 24 hour lifecycle rule, an IAM prefix condition, and object-level logging on deletion.
P6Unattributable change4 or 8 to 16MediumHighWithout CloudTrail, GuardDuty or Config, a change to the account leaves no trustworthy record.Enable all three. This is the precondition for every other claim, and the shortest path to a SOC 2 window.
What the five scores meanhow each axis was judged
1
ExploitabilityWhat the attacker needs. A forwarded link needs nothing; a supply-chain compromise needs a great deal. This is the axis a penetration test would move most.
2
ExposureHow reachable the first stage is from outside, using only what is publicly discoverable: DNS, certificate transparency, a sign-in page, a package registry.
3
Likelihood of attackHow often this class of thing happens to platforms built this way. Leaked keys and forwarded links are ordinary; image substitution is not.
4
SeverityThe technical outcome if the path completes: what is read, changed, or made unavailable.
5
ImpactWhat it costs the business. Cross-tenant disclosure of customer content scores highest here even where exploitability is low, because it is the incident a platform rarely survives intact.
·
These are judgement, not arithmeticNo CVSS vector is implied. The scores exist to order the work, and the ordering is the point: the highest-scoring paths on both platforms are broken by changes that are configuration rather than rearchitecture.
Overall severityrisk per path, and where the platform sits

Risk is likelihood multiplied by consequence, on the same 1 to 5 scale. Likelihood is the mean of exploitability, exposure and likelihood of attack; consequence is the mean of severity and impact. Bands: under 2 guarded, 2 to 3 moderate, 3 to 4 elevated, 4 and above high.

PathOverall riskWhat drives it
P1Stolen token to cross-tenant evidence4.3 highBoth likelihood and impact are at their ceiling. A stolen session is ordinary, and the boundary beneath it is application code.
P2Share link replay4.2 highExploitability is 5: a forwarded link needs no account, no session and no skill.
P3Pipeline to scan task2.3 moderateLow likelihood, maximum consequence. This is the path you accept and monitor rather than the one you fix first.
P4Scan tier to data tier2.1 moderateThe scan tier is designed to run hostile input, and it shares a subnet with the API.
P5Target credential reuse2.4 moderateThe window is short, but the credential belongs to the customer, not to you.
P6Unattributable change2.1 moderateNot an attack in itself. It is the reason you could not answer questions about any of the others.

Platform position: High. Litmus sits at High overall, driven entirely by P1 and P2. Both are paths into another tenant’s evidence, and both are severed by changes that are configuration rather than rearchitecture. With those two closed the platform drops to Moderate, because everything remaining needs either pipeline access or a foothold inside the VPC.

Recommended mitigations and remediationsin the order I would do them

Ordered by what each one closes for what it costs, not by severity. Three of the first four are configuration and cost nothing but time. Each row names the paths it removes, so the table can be read against the graph above.

RemediationPaths it closesEffortCostWhenWhy this one
1Row-level security in PostgresP1, narrows P4MediumNonePhase 1Policies on every tenant table with the organisation set per connection. A forgotten filter returns zero rows instead of another tenant’s findings.
2Short-lived, one-time report linksP2LowNonePhase 1A short TTL, tokens bound to a recipient, tokens out of the query string, and object-level logging so a read is a recorded event.
3Enable CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config and Security HubP6Low150 to 400 a monthPhase 1The detective floor. Nothing else on this list can be evidenced without it, and it is the shortest path to a SOC 2 observation window.
4Dedicated subnet, security group and egress allowlist for the scan tierP4MediumSmallPhase 2No route from the scan tier to the data tier, and no arbitrary egress from a container that runs attacker payloads by design.
5Scoped per-scan role with session tagsP3, P5MediumNonePhase 2Move RunTask and SES off the task role. A scan should be able to read its own config, write its own prefix and invoke the model, and nothing else.
6Separate configs bucket with a lifecycle rule and a prefix conditionP5LowNonePhase 2Target credentials stop sharing a bucket with evidence, and expire on a clock rather than on the application remembering to delete them.
7Pin dependencies, sign images, verify at deployP3MediumNonePhase 3Closes the gap between what the pipeline built and what runs. Add Inspector on the registry for what the signature cannot tell you.
8Macie on the report bucketinforms P1 and P2LowUsage basedPhase 3Answers whether reports actually hold regulated data rather than assuming they might. Changes what the first two rows cost.
Mitigation, remediation, or acceptedhow to read the colours on the overlay

The overlay separates three things that often get called the same word. Green removes the cause, amber reduces the chance or the damage, grey means there is no fix and the risk is managed instead.

R
Remediation, greenRemoves the cause. After it lands the hop is no longer available: a forgotten filter returns nothing, an unsigned image will not deploy, a revoked key stops resolving.
M
Mitigation, amberReduces the chance or the blast radius without removing the hop. Shorter sessions, tighter TTLs, alerting, logging. Useful, and not the same thing as a fix.
A
Accepted, greyTwo stages carry no fix at all. The Septa proxy must hold plaintext to inspect it, and prompt evasion is an open research problem. These are properties of the design, so they are managed rather than closed.
✓
This sufficesOne control per path carries the label. It is the single change that drops the path to its residual score on its own. The others still earn their place, but if you do one thing on that row, do the badged one.
Which one would sufficeone control per path, and why that one

Every row on the figure carries a THIS SUFFICES badge on a single control. This is that list. Each of these on its own takes the path to the residual score shown beside it.

The one that sufficesKindWhy this one
P1Row-level security on every tenant tableremediationA stolen token stops being a way into another tenant. The other three controls narrow the window; this one closes the door.
P2One-time tokens bound to a recipientremediationA forwarded link stops being a credential. Short TTLs help, but a link that works twice is the whole problem.
P3Sign with cosign and verify at deployremediationWhat runs becomes provably what was built. Pinned dependencies reduce the odds; verification removes the hop.
P4A dedicated subnet and security group for the scan tierremediationThe scan tier keeps running hostile input, which is its job, but it can no longer reach the data tier.
P5A separate configs bucket with a lifecycle ruleremediationTarget credentials stop sharing a bucket with evidence and expire on a clock rather than on the application remembering.
P6An organisation trail to a locked bucketremediationEverything else on this row is a detail once changes are attributable.
How to use thismethod, scope and honesty

Where the content comes fromThe architecture views in this document, not a scan. Every node is a component or a control that already appears in OV-1, SV-1 or the overlays, so the graph and the diagrams cannot drift apart.
2
What counts as externally availableDNS, certificate transparency, the public endpoints themselves, the identity provider on the sign-in page, package and image registries, and the vendor documentation for each subprocessor. No credentialed testing is assumed.
3
How exploitability was judgedBy what a path needs: a stolen credential, a forwarded link, a dependency, or nothing but a valid account. Paths needing only things that leak in ordinary operation are rated higher than paths needing a supply-chain compromise.
4
What this is notNot a penetration test and not a vulnerability assessment. There is no CVE here because the exposure is architectural: controls applied in application code, or not yet applied at all. A test would confirm these, not discover them.
5
What to do with itWork the What breaks it column, not the graph. Six of the thirteen paths are severed by four changes: row-level security, short-lived report links, mTLS on the internal hop, and enabling the detective trio.

Septa threat model and attack graph

The same four bands applied to the proxy. Septa stores no customer content, so the impact column is about content in flight, provider spend, and the ability to prove what happened.

Attack paths, scoredseven paths, each read left to right, with five scores
View
External exposurewhat is reachable, and what it tells an attacker

The starting column of the graph, in words. Everything here is discoverable without touching the platform: DNS records, certificate transparency, a sign-in page, a support ticket.

What it isWhy it matters
Proxy endpointapi.septa.prompthalo.dev on CloudFront, WAF proposed but not deployedOne public hostname for every tenant. Discoverable from DNS and certificate transparency.
Customer API keysone key resolves to one tenant, cached for 60 secondsThe root of the whole tenancy boundary. Keys leak into repositories, logs and support tickets more often than they are stolen.
Operator consoleRuntime Defense, where policy changes without a deployA change here alters enforcement for every tenant, and today leaves no account-level record.
Delivery chainGitHub Actions, ECR, and the OIDC trust policyNo static AWS key, which is the right design. The remaining risk is what gets built, since nothing signs or scans the image.
Provider egressone NAT gateway to OpenAI, Anthropic and othersThe only hop on which customer content leaves AWS, and a single point of failure for availability.
Attack paths in table formthe same seven paths, for a questionnaire

Ratings are judgement, not arithmetic. Likelihood is how often this class of thing happens to platforms built this way; impact is what it costs if it does. Nothing here needs a zero day.

PathChainLikelihoodImpactWhat happensWhat breaks it
Q1Key leak to content disclosure2 to 5 to 9 to 13HighSevereA leaked API key authenticates as a tenant; the proxy holds plaintext for every tenant in the same process.Per-tenant rate limits, a push-based revocation that beats the cache, and key scanning in CI and the repositories.
Q2Revocation window5 to 10 to 13HighHighA revoked key keeps resolving for up to 60 seconds because the identity cache is TTL-based.Publish an invalidation on revocation rather than waiting out the TTL. Cheap, and customers ask about it.
Q3Internal hop interception7 to 9 to 13MediumSevereCloudFront to the ALB runs on port 80, so content is readable in a second place inside the VPC.mTLS on the internal hop, which is what ACM Private CA was for. This is SEPTA-91.
Q4Unsigned image to code execution4 to 8 to 9MediumSevereNothing signs or scans an image between build and run, so what runs is not provably what was built.Sign with cosign and verify at deploy, and add Inspector scanning on the registry.
Q5Policy bypass1 to 6 to 9MediumHighA prompt crafted to evade the pattern index reaches a provider despite the policy.Treat detection coverage as a versioned claim, add per-tenant overlays, and record which index version produced each verdict.
Q6Noisy tenant to availability5 to 12 to 16MediumHighNo per-tenant rate limit or concurrency budget, so one tenant’s load is every tenant’s latency.A token bucket per tenant at the proxy. This is an isolation control, not a billing one.
Q7Provider spend5 or 11 to 14MediumHighSepta holds every provider credential so customers do not have to. That is a real gain and a concentration of risk.Per-tenant secret paths, a published rotation interval, and a customer-supplied key option.
What the five scores meanhow each axis was judged
1
ExploitabilityWhat the attacker needs. A forwarded link needs nothing; a supply-chain compromise needs a great deal. This is the axis a penetration test would move most.
2
ExposureHow reachable the first stage is from outside, using only what is publicly discoverable: DNS, certificate transparency, a sign-in page, a package registry.
3
Likelihood of attackHow often this class of thing happens to platforms built this way. Leaked keys and forwarded links are ordinary; image substitution is not.
4
SeverityThe technical outcome if the path completes: what is read, changed, or made unavailable.
5
ImpactWhat it costs the business. Cross-tenant disclosure of customer content scores highest here even where exploitability is low, because it is the incident a platform rarely survives intact.
·
These are judgement, not arithmeticNo CVSS vector is implied. The scores exist to order the work, and the ordering is the point: the highest-scoring paths on both platforms are broken by changes that are configuration rather than rearchitecture.
Overall severityrisk per path, and where the platform sits

Risk is likelihood multiplied by consequence, on the same 1 to 5 scale. Likelihood is the mean of exploitability, exposure and likelihood of attack; consequence is the mean of severity and impact. Bands: under 2 guarded, 2 to 3 moderate, 3 to 4 elevated, 4 and above high.

PathOverall riskWhat drives it
Q1Key leak to content disclosure4.3 highOne leaked key reaches a process holding plaintext for every tenant at the same moment.
Q2Revocation window2.8 moderateA customer believes revocation is immediate. For up to 60 seconds it is not.
Q3Internal hop interception2.0 moderateHard to reach, but the consequence is a second readable copy of customer content inside the VPC.
Q4Unsigned image to code execution2.3 moderateNeeds pipeline access, and then the attacker is the proxy.
Q5Policy bypass3.0 elevatedHigh exposure and high likelihood, lower consequence: the call goes through, and the audit trail records that it did.
Q6Noisy tenant to availability1.8 guardedAvailability rather than confidentiality, but it hits every tenant at once.
Q7Provider spend2.3 moderateSepta holds every provider credential so customers do not have to. That is a real gain and a real concentration.

Platform position: High. Septa sits at High overall on the strength of Q1 alone. Every other path is Moderate or below, which is a consequence of the design: there is no customer content at rest to steal. Close Q1 and Q5 and the platform drops to Moderate, and the residual risk becomes availability and spend rather than confidentiality.

Recommended mitigations and remediationsin the order I would do them

Ordered by what each one closes for what it costs, not by severity. Three of the first four are configuration and cost nothing but time. Each row names the paths it removes, so the table can be read against the graph above.

RemediationPaths it closesEffortCostWhenWhy this one
1Push-based revocationQ2LowNonePhase 1Publish an invalidation when a key is revoked instead of waiting out the sixty second cache. Customers ask about this window by name.
2Per-tenant rate limits and concurrency budgetsQ6, narrows Q1MediumNonePhase 1A token bucket per tenant at the proxy. This is an isolation control, not a billing one: one tenant’s load is currently every tenant’s latency.
3Enable CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Configthe unlogged-change impactLow100 to 300 a monthPhase 1Policy changes from the operator console currently leave no account-level record. This is what makes them attributable.
4mTLS on the internal hopQ3MediumAbout 400 a month for Private CAPhase 2ACM Private CA exists for this and is disabled. It removes the second place content is readable, and closes SEPTA-91.
5Sign images, verify at deploy, scan in ECRQ4MediumSmallPhase 2What runs becomes provably what was built. Without it, the strongest control on the platform runs unverified code.
6Key hygiene: scanning, per-tenant secret paths, rotationQ1, Q7LowNonePhase 2Most keys leak rather than get stolen. Scan the repositories and CI, split the secret paths, and publish the rotation interval.
7Version the detection claim, add per-tenant overlaysQ5MediumNonePhase 3Record which index version produced each verdict, so a coverage change is explainable rather than a silent regression.
8Offer a customer-supplied provider keyQ7MediumNonePhase 3The customer keeps their own provider credential and Septa never holds it. Removes the concentration for the customers who care about it.
Mitigation, remediation, or acceptedhow to read the colours on the overlay

The overlay separates three things that often get called the same word. Green removes the cause, amber reduces the chance or the damage, grey means there is no fix and the risk is managed instead.

R
Remediation, greenRemoves the cause. After it lands the hop is no longer available: a forgotten filter returns nothing, an unsigned image will not deploy, a revoked key stops resolving.
M
Mitigation, amberReduces the chance or the blast radius without removing the hop. Shorter sessions, tighter TTLs, alerting, logging. Useful, and not the same thing as a fix.
A
Accepted, greyTwo stages carry no fix at all. The Septa proxy must hold plaintext to inspect it, and prompt evasion is an open research problem. These are properties of the design, so they are managed rather than closed.
✓
This sufficesOne control per path carries the badge. It is the single change that drops the path to its residual score on its own. The others still earn their place, but if you do one thing on that row, do the badged one.
Which one would sufficeone control per path, and why that one

Every row on the figure carries a THIS SUFFICES badge on a single control. This is that list. Each of these on its own takes the path to the residual score shown beside it.

The one that sufficesKindWhy this one
Q1Secret scanning in CI and in the repositoriesremediationMost keys leak rather than get stolen. Removing the leak is worth more than anything downstream of it.
Q2Publish an invalidation on revocationremediationThe sixty second window disappears. Shortening the TTL only makes it smaller.
Q3mTLS with ACM Private CAremediationThe second readable copy of content inside the VPC goes away. This is SEPTA-91, and it is the only fix on this row.
Q4Verify the signature at deployremediationSigning without verifying changes nothing. The verification is the control.
Q5Report coverage as a dated claimmitigationNo remediation exists. Evasion is an open problem, so the honest control is to version the claim and say when it was measured.
Q6A token bucket per tenant at the proxyremediationOne tenant stops being every tenant’s latency. Autoscaling only buys time.
Q7Offer a customer-supplied provider keyremediationFor the customers who ask, the concentration disappears entirely because Septa never holds the credential.

About the icons. These are SVG icons drawn in the AWS Architecture Icons visual language, category colour, rounded tile, white glyph, not the licensed asset files from the official AWS set. They print cleanly at any size and are safe in internal and client documents. Every diagram references them by id, so swapping in the official marks is one edit per icon in the symbol block at the top of this file. Third-party services appear as monogram tiles in brand colours rather than reproduced logos.

About the overlays. The base architecture is a reading of the Litmus technical architecture document, staging branch, 2026-08-27. The data, protocol and encryption overlays restate what that document states. The Well-Architected and security overlays are interpretation: the amber items are questions for a design review, not findings about the running system.
